title: Office Space
logline: Fed-up software engineers scheme against their company. Deadpan workplace satire.
overview: A depressed white-collar worker tries hypnotherapy, only to find himself in a perpetual state of devil-may-care bliss that prompts him to start living by his own rules, and hatch a hapless attempt to embezzle money from his soul-killing employers.

jokes.text: White-collar office worker stuck in traffic jams up aggressive gangsta rap, turns it down to speak, then cranks it back up — suburban commuter performing street identity
jokes.setup: Aggressive gangsta rap plays loudly in what is clearly a mundane suburban traffic jam; lyrics threaten violence and assert dominance
jokes.punchline: Peter turns it down to speak, then turns it back up — a mild, frustrated white-collar guy fully embodying the song as an emotional outlet before returning to helpless gridlock
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of violent gangsta rap as the emotional anthem of a suburban software drone stuck in traffic is a sharp, economical piece of character-establishment comedy. The turn-down-to-talk / turn-back-up choreography is a perfect visual punchline that shows Mike Judge's precise control of the gag without over-explaining it. The character integration is excellent — it only works because we immediately understand who Peter is.

jokes.text: Peter, still stuck in traffic, mutters fragmented profanity — 'Mother...shittin'...son of a--Ass! Ooh! I just...' — a string of incomplete obscenities delivered to no one
jokes.setup: Peter is visibly losing his mind in bumper-to-bumper traffic
jokes.punchline: His rage is so total it can't even form complete sentences — he cycles through partial swear words and trails off helplessly
jokes.explanation: The fragmented profanity is a recognizable and well-observed portrait of commuter-rage implosion. It's funny because his frustration exceeds language itself. Solid character work but not particularly original — this is a well-worn comedic mode.

jokes.text: Peter, arriving late, recites in a robotic panic: 'I was told that if I was late again I would be summarily dismissed' — the word 'summarily' in a stream of anxious rambling
jokes.setup: Peter is rushing into the office after the traffic ordeal, clearly frazzled
jokes.punchline: His use of the formal corporate word 'summarily dismissed' in the middle of a panicked mutter perfectly captures the way corporate-speak has colonized even his private anxiety
jokes.explanation: A quiet but accurate joke about how corporate language infiltrates internal monologue. Competent but understated — it's more of a texture joke than a big laugh.

jokes.text: Peter sets his car alarm in the parking lot — the visual irony of a man stressed about being late taking the time to set an alarm on his beaten-up commuter car
jokes.setup: Peter is panicked about being late and fired
jokes.punchline: He pauses to set his car alarm anyway — a mundane ritual that undercuts the urgency and implies his car is not worth protecting
jokes.explanation: A mild visual gag that extends the film's thesis about mindless routine overriding rational priority. Functional but low-impact — the kind of observational beat that lands a small smile rather than a laugh.

jokes.text: Nina answers the phone in a relentless loop: 'Corporate accounts payable. Nina speaking. Just a moment.' — repeated five times without pause or variation
jokes.setup: We enter the office and hear Nina on the phone
jokes.punchline: The gag is the loop itself — she is a human answering machine, the same four words cycling endlessly, a perfect portrait of dehumanizing corporate work
jokes.explanation: One of the film's most precise satirical jokes. The structure — exact repetition with zero variation — IS the joke. It needs no punchline beyond itself; the repetition communicates total spiritual vacancy. The economy is extraordinary: nine words repeated five times says everything about what it means to work a soul-crushing clerical job. It recurs throughout the film as a running gag, adding rewatch value.

jokes.text: Bill Lumbergh arrives mid-Nina loop and says 'Hello, Peter. What's happening?' in his signature slow, nasal drawl — the absolute banality of his greeting against the background drone of Nina's phone loop
jokes.setup: Nina's dehumanizing phone loop has set a tone of corporate drone existence; we now meet the boss
jokes.punchline: Lumbergh's greeting — 'Hello, Peter. What's happening?' — is delivered with the same vacant, performatively casual affect that will define every interaction with him. It's friendly in form, threatening in function.
jokes.explanation: Bill Lumbergh is one of cinema's great comic creations, and this is his introduction. 'What's happening?' is a masterclass in passive-aggressive corporate-speak — the words are casual but every employee immediately understands it means trouble. The character integration score is near-perfect: no other character could deliver this line this way. The slow drawl, the coffee mug, the total unawareness of his own menace — this is the joke. It instantly establishes the film's central comedic antagonist and the specific flavor of dread he produces.

jokes.text: Bill explains the TPS report cover sheet issue in excruciating, repetitive corporate non-speak: 'If you could just go ahead and make sure you do that from now on, that would be great...' — extended to absurdity
jokes.setup: Peter forgot a cover sheet on a TPS report — a trivial clerical mistake
jokes.punchline: Bill's response is disproportionately elaborate, full of corporate softeners ('sort of,' 'just go ahead,' 'that would be great') that make a nothing issue feel like a formal disciplinary proceeding
jokes.explanation: The TPS report scene is the film's most iconic workplace comedy set piece. The humor is precisely calibrated: the issue is completely trivial (a cover sheet), the language is laboriously passive-aggressive, and Peter's growing frustration ('I have the memo right here') is perfectly rendered. 'That would be great' became a cultural touchstone for a reason — it distills an entire species of corporate management communication into five words. The extended, non-economical explanation IS the comedic economy; the bloat is the point.

jokes.text: Bill cuts Peter off mid-protest about having the memo to immediately pivot to: 'Hello, Phil. What's happening?' — beginning the exact same TPS conversation with someone else
jokes.setup: Peter is trying to explain he has the memo; Bill appears to be listening
jokes.punchline: Bill simply turns to the next person and begins the exact same scripted conversation — Peter didn't even register as a human being to him
jokes.explanation: The pivot to Phil is the perfect punchline to the entire Lumbergh introduction. The joke isn't just that he dismisses Peter — it's that he is running the SAME interaction in parallel, serially, robotically. He is not a manager; he is a process. The economy of the joke is superb: no extra words, just the identical greeting to a new person. This clarifies everything about Lumbergh in one beat and is the moment the character fully clicks as a comic creation.

jokes.text: Milton's negotiation over radio volume: 'I was told that I could listen to the radio at a reasonable volume from 9:00 to 11:00' — the specificity of '9:00 to 11:00' and 'reasonable volume' as sacred written-in-law
jokes.setup: Peter asks Milton to turn down the radio as a personal favor
jokes.punchline: Milton invokes a formal prior agreement about listening rights with bureaucratic precision, treating a minor office courtesy as a legal matter requiring documented precedent
jokes.explanation: Milton's introduction is excellent character comedy. His insistence on the exact parameters of his radio agreement — time-stamped, volume-qualified, negotiated against Sandra's headphone usage — reveals a man living in a web of micro-grievances and bureaucratic self-protection. The character integration is near-perfect: this is Milton's entire personality compressed into one exchange.

jokes.text: Dom Portwood approaches Peter about TPS reports — the exact same conversation as Bill's, beat for beat, including 'Did you get that memo?'
jokes.setup: Peter has already had the TPS conversation with Bill and tried to end it
jokes.punchline: Dom begins the same conversation verbatim — TPS reports, cover sheets, the memo — proving this is a systemic condition, not one manager's quirk
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the TPS gag from one manager to two (and then hinted at via phone in the next beat) is a structural masterstroke. The joke is no longer about Bill being annoying — it's about a system that processes its humans through identical loops. The escalation lands harder than the original because we now understand the full horror. 'That'd be great' reappears as a callback punchline.

jokes.text: Peter answers the phone and says 'I have the memo' preemptively — before the caller has said anything about TPS reports
jokes.setup: Peter has now had the TPS conversation twice in quick succession
jokes.punchline: He answers the phone with 'I have the memo' — the TPS harassment has conditioned him to assume every incoming call is about the cover sheet
jokes.explanation: Three words — 'I have the memo' — are the perfect payoff to the entire TPS sequence. The economy is exceptional: no setup needed, no explanation. The audience has been primed by two identical conversations and Peter's escalating frustration, so this pre-emptive defense lands as a genuine surprise that also feels completely inevitable. It's arguably the best single line in this reel — a callback that completes the joke structure with maximum efficiency.

jokes.text: Samir rages at the printer: 'Why does it say paper jam when there is no paper jam? I swear to God, one of these days I just kick this piece of shit out the window.'
jokes.setup: Samir is at the office printer, which has apparently jammed with no discernible cause
jokes.punchline: His rage is completely disproportionate and entirely relatable — the printer has beaten him again, and he invokes defenestration as the logical solution
jokes.explanation: Seeds the printer destruction scene that becomes one of the film's most iconic sequences. Here it's a solid observational joke about the specific rage of a fake paper jam — universally relatable, well-delivered, sets up future payoff. The rewatch bonus is high because viewers know what's coming.

jokes.text: Peggy attempts to read Samir's last name from a document: 'Samir... Na-Na... Na-Naga--' — trails off helplessly
jokes.setup: Peggy has a document and is trying to read Samir's last name aloud
jokes.punchline: She gets three syllables in and completely loses the ability to continue, leaving Samir to cut her off with a resigned 'No. Thanks.'
jokes.explanation: A cringey but accurate joke about the experience of having an unfamiliar name in a homogeneous workplace. The structure is good — Peggy's attempt is sincere, which makes the failure worse. Samir's 'No. Thanks.' is a perfect economy of resignation. Some may find it dated.

jokes.text: Peggy reads 'Michael Bolton?' with delighted recognition, as if meeting a celebrity
jokes.setup: Immediately after failing to read Samir's name, Peggy gets to the next name on her list
jokes.punchline: She lights up at 'Michael Bolton' — the contrast between her failure on Samir's name and her instant, enthusiastic recognition of the celebrity-adjacent name is the joke
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition with the previous beat makes this land harder than it would alone. The irony is clean: the name that causes Samir daily indignity goes unread, while Michael's name — which causes HIM daily indignity via celebrity confusion — is immediately recognizable and celebrated.

jokes.text: Michael: 'There was nothing wrong with it until I was about twelve years old and that no-talent ass clown became famous and started winning Grammys.'
jokes.setup: Samir suggests there's nothing wrong with the name Michael Bolton
jokes.punchline: Michael's furious, specific, deeply personal grievance about the singer — the phrase 'no-talent ass clown' delivered with genuine venom — is the full comedic payload
jokes.explanation: 'No-talent ass clown' is legitimately one of the most quotable phrases in the film and among the great comedic insults in 90s cinema. The specificity of 'started winning Grammys' — that the Grammys is what really stings — is perfect character work. This is a highly quotable, specific, well-constructed joke with excellent character integration.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Why should I change? He's the one who sucks.'
jokes.setup: Samir suggests Michael just go by 'Mike' instead of 'Michael' to avoid confusion with the singer
jokes.punchline: Michael's refusal is framed as a principled stand — HE should not have to change his name because the other Michael Bolton is the inferior one
jokes.explanation: One of the film's best lines. 'Why should I change? He's the one who sucks.' achieves near-perfect comedic economy — nine words that contain a complete, inverted logic, a character portrait, and a callback punchline. The structure is flawless: Samir's reasonable suggestion sets up an entirely unreasonable but completely internally-consistent refusal. The character integration is exceptional — this is a line that could only come from this exact character in this exact situation. It is very close to the 8.0 anchor in quality and arguably exceeds it in quotability.

jokes.text: Waitress at Chotchkie's: 'Sounds like somebody's got a case of the Mondays!' — said to Peter who has just mimed machine-gunning his workplace
jokes.setup: Peter has just vented about his miserable day and mimed shooting his coworkers with a machine gun, laughing nervously
jokes.punchline: The waitress, apparently trained in relentless corporate-enforced positivity, responds with the most anodyne possible phrase — 'case of the Mondays' — which is both wildly insufficient and perfectly captures the dehumanizing customer-service script
jokes.explanation: The 'case of the Mondays' gag is clever on two levels: it's the kind of chirpy service-industry phrase that is itself a minor workplace indignity, AND it foreshadows the Lawrence scene where Peter discovers that only corporate environments use this phrase. The setup (Peter miming a machine gun) makes the waitress's response land especially well.

jokes.text: Peter's machine-gun mime: 'One of these days it's just gonna be like--' [imitates machine gun] followed by nervous laughter
jokes.setup: Peter is venting about his terrible day to Michael and Samir at Chotchkie's
jokes.punchline: He mimes shooting his workplace with a machine gun as a punchline to 'some days' — a recognizable outlet-of-last-resort for workplace frustration, delivered with enough earnestness to be slightly unsettling
jokes.explanation: A functional workplace-frustration joke that works primarily as a setup for the waitress's 'case of the Mondays' line. The machine-gun mime itself isn't especially original — it's a common expression of frustration — but it's well-deployed here as a contrast for what follows.

jokes.text: Michael: 'What if we're still doing this when we're fifty?' / Samir: 'It would be nice to have that kind of job security.'
jokes.setup: Peter has expressed existential dread about his dead-end job
jokes.punchline: Samir reframes 'still doing this at fifty' — which Michael meant as a horror — as a desirable indicator of job security. The deadpan sincerity makes it land.
jokes.explanation: A sharp little irony. Samir's response is a perfect deadpan inversion — the dystopia Peter dreads is recoded as the aspiration Samir envies. It's a good two-line joke that efficiently characterizes both the anxiety (Michael) and the immigrant-worker pragmatism (Samir) in the film's worldview.

jokes.text: Peter: 'I'm a big pussy, which is why I work at Initech to begin with.'
jokes.setup: Peter explains why he'll end up working the Saturday Lumbergh wants
jokes.punchline: He delivers a clinical self-diagnosis — 'I'm a big pussy' — with the same flat resignation as a doctor reading test results, extending it to explain his entire career trajectory
jokes.explanation: Peter's self-aware self-loathing is a good character note — the joke is that he articulates it so precisely and without any defensive spin. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Michael: 'They don't understand. I could program a virus that'd rip that place off big time. Big time.'
jokes.setup: Michael is insisting Initech will find out the hard way that he's not a pushover
jokes.punchline: His threat — a virus — is characteristically nerd-specific, and 'big time. Big time.' (repeated) undercuts any menace with its awkward emphasis
jokes.explanation: Seeds the actual virus plot that becomes the film's central scheme — rewatch bonus is high. The 'big time. Big time.' repetition is a character-specific verbal tic that undercuts the threat nicely. Functional setup joke.

jokes.text: Peter's excuse for not asking out the waitress: 'I'm just another asshole customer. You can't just walk up to a waitress and ask her out.'
jokes.setup: Samir notes Peter stares at the waitress every time they come in and suggests he ask her out
jokes.punchline: Peter's reasoning — the elaborate social prohibition on asking out service workers — is simultaneously a recognizable rationalization and a bit absurd given that the prohibition is entirely invented by him
jokes.explanation: A competent observational joke about romantic passivity. It's accurate but not particularly original — this kind of self-imposed social prohibition is a well-worn comedic territory.

jokes.text: Peter mentions he's going to an 'occupational hypnotherapist' with Anne
jokes.setup: Peter is explaining why he can't play poker on Friday
jokes.punchline: The punchline is the specific phrase 'occupational hypnotherapist' — a real but inherently comedic subspecialty that sounds like something Anne invented
jokes.explanation: A setup joke that pays off later in the film with the actual hypnotherapy session. The humor is in the specificity — not just a hypnotherapist but an OCCUPATIONAL one, implying Peter's spiritual crisis has been professionally categorized. Good setup.

jokes.text: Peter says the hypnotherapist 'really helped Anne lose weight' — Samir: 'Peter, she's anorexic.' / Peter: 'Yeah, I know. The guy's really good.'
jokes.setup: Peter is defending the occupational hypnotherapist's credentials by citing Anne's weight loss
jokes.punchline: Samir points out Anne is anorexic — the weight loss is not a therapeutic success but a symptom of an eating disorder. Peter's response ('Yeah, I know. The guy's really good.') confirms he understands this and still counts it as an endorsement.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in this reel. The structure is perfect: Peter presents a testimonial, Samir reveals it's pathological, and Peter's 'Yeah, I know. The guy's really good.' — confirming he has fully processed the information and arrived at the wrong conclusion — is the ideal punchline. It's dark, economical, and reveals something true and terrible about Peter's character (he's not malicious, he's just profoundly not paying attention). The craft is high — this is close to the 8.0 anchor in structure.

jokes.text: Samir's TPS report callback at Chotchkie's: 'Hey, and speaking of problems, what's this I hear about you having problems with your TPS reports?' / 'Yeah. Didn't you get that memo?'
jokes.setup: The guys are having a relaxed conversation at their lunch spot, ostensibly a refuge from office stress
jokes.punchline: Samir brings up the TPS reports — unprompted, at Chotchkie's — and Michael delivers the 'didn't you get that memo?' line, now fully a running gag punchline
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback that shows the TPS memo gag has legs beyond the office. The joke is that even outside the building, in their lunch haven, the corporate drone keeps following them. The 'didn't you get that memo' punchline is now doing running-gag duty effectively.

jokes.text: Tom Smykowski runs across the parking lot to find the guys, visibly hyperventilating, apparently having had a minor cardiac event
jokes.setup: The guys are relaxing at Chotchkie's
jokes.punchline: Tom's physical entrance — running and panting — is immediately diagnosed by Michael: 'Oh, probably working on another heart attack.' Implying this is a known, recurring behavior.
jokes.explanation: 'Probably working on another heart attack' is a good line — the word 'another' implies a history. Tom's physical comedy (panting, frantic) works in context. Solid character introduction.

jokes.text: Tom: 'You know, there are people in this world who don't have to put up with all this shit? Like that guy that invented the pet rock.'
jokes.setup: Tom is spiraling about the layoff threat
jokes.punchline: He invokes the pet rock inventor as the gold standard of human freedom — the ideal life is not a great career but a single moronic idea that made millions
jokes.explanation: The pet rock reference is a good comedic choice — it's the ultimate symbol of pointless wealth creation, and Tom's delivery of it as serious life philosophy reveals his desperation. The jump from 'consultants may fire me' to 'like the pet rock guy' is an excellent comedic non-sequitur.

jokes.text: Tom unveils his idea: a 'Jump to Conclusions' mat — a mat with conclusions written on it that you jump to
jokes.setup: Tom has built to a dramatic reveal of his million-dollar idea, the equivalent of the pet rock
jokes.punchline: The 'Jump to Conclusions' mat is a literal, physical realization of a figure of speech — it is at once completely logical and completely idiotic
jokes.explanation: The Jump to Conclusions mat is one of the film's signature jokes and among the best absurdist comedy bits in 1990s cinema. The comedic concept is brilliant: it takes an idiom literally and constructs a physical product around it. The escalating explanation — 'it would have different conclusions on it... that you could jump to' — delivered with complete earnestness by Tom, while Michael and Samir's silence communicates total horror, is structurally flawless. The beat of silence before Michael's verdict ('That is the worst idea I've ever heard in my life') is perfectly timed. This is legitimately close to the 9+ tier of comedy — it's specific, original, structurally perfect, and has entered cultural vocabulary.

jokes.text: Tom's 'Jump to Conclusions Mat' pitch: 'It would be this mat that you would put on the floor, and it would have different conclusions written on it, that you could jump to.'
jokes.setup: Tom says he once had a great million-dollar idea
jokes.punchline: The 'Jump to Conclusions Mat' — a literal mat you jump to conclusions on — is a physical product version of an idiom, as moronic as it sounds, and Tom delivers it with complete earnestness
jokes.explanation: One of the most beloved jokes in the film and a genuine 8+ moment. The 'Jump to Conclusions Mat' works on multiple levels: (1) it makes literal a figurative expression, which is a classic absurdist technique; (2) the explanation is delivered with total sincerity and architectural detail — 'that you would put on the floor, and it would have different conclusions written on it, that you could jump to' — the earnest elaboration is structurally perfect because each additional detail makes it MORE ridiculous; (3) the pause before Michael and Samir's reactions ('That is the worst idea I've ever heard in my life, Tom' / 'Yes. Yes, it's horrible, this idea.') is comedy timing gold. The idea is so specifically stupid that it transcends generic. Fully earns 8+.

jokes.text: Michael: 'That is the worst idea I've ever heard in my life, Tom.' / Samir: 'Yes. Yes, it's horrible, this idea.'
jokes.setup: Tom has just finished explaining the Jump to Conclusions mat with complete sincerity
jokes.punchline: The double condemnation — Michael's flat finality, Samir's slightly delayed and syntactically formal concurrence — is perfectly calibrated. Neither raises their voice; both simply state the verdict.
jokes.explanation: The punchline to the Jump to Conclusions mat. 'That is the worst idea I've ever heard in my life' has the structure of an absolute verdict, and Samir's 'Yes. Yes, it's horrible, this idea.' — with its inverted syntax — lands as a character-specific flourish. The double beat and the absence of any softening or hedging is what makes it work. The reaction IS the punchline.

jokes.text: Michael's deconstruction of the guidance counselor career exercise: 'No, you're working at Initech because that question is bullshit to begin with. If everyone listened to her, there'd be no janitors, because no one would clean shit if they had a million dollars.'
jokes.setup: Peter says he never had an answer to the guidance counselor's 'what would you do with a million dollars' question, and that's why he's at Initech
jokes.punchline: Michael's rebuttal — that the question is structurally flawed because it assumes everyone's dream job is socially necessary — arrives at 'no one would clean shit' as its logical terminus
jokes.explanation: A genuinely sharp piece of observational comedy about the fundamental flaw in the 'follow your dreams' career mythology. The logic is airtight — the system depends on people doing jobs no one would choose — and 'clean shit' is the perfect, blunt endpoint. Character integration is good: this is exactly how Michael thinks.

jokes.text: Samir's response to 'what would you do with a million dollars': 'I would invest half of it in glorious mutual funds and then take the other half to my friend Asadulah who works in securities--'
jokes.setup: Michael asks Samir what he'd do with a million dollars, expecting a fun fantasy answer
jokes.punchline: Samir immediately pivots to a detailed, entirely practical investment strategy — 'glorious mutual funds' — missing the point of the exercise entirely and revealing his immigrant-pragmatist personality
jokes.explanation: 'Glorious mutual funds' is a wonderful phrase — the word 'glorious' applied to mutual funds captures Samir's reverence for financial security in a way that's both funny and character-specific. The practical investment answer to what is meant to be a fantasy question is excellent character comedy. The reference to 'my friend Asadulah who works in securities' adds another layer of specificity.

jokes.text: Printer displays 'PC LOAD LETTER' — Samir stops mid-sentence and says 'PC load letter? What the fuck does that mean?'
jokes.setup: Michael is explaining why Samir is missing the point of the million-dollars exercise
jokes.punchline: The printer interrupts a philosophical conversation with its inscrutable error message — Samir abandons the conversation entirely to confront the printer, the mundane technology crisis taking priority over all else
jokes.explanation: A callback to the printer frustration, elevated by its comedic timing — the printer interrupts a mid-sentence philosophical point. 'What the fuck does that mean?' is both Samir's reasonable question about an absurd error message AND a commentary on the entire experience of office technology. High quotability: 'PC load letter' became a genuine cultural reference.

jokes.text: Lawrence yells through the wall: 'Hey Peter, man! Check out channel nine! Check out this chick!' — from a neighbor Peter can clearly hear through thin apartment walls
jokes.setup: Peter has arrived home and turned on the TV
jokes.punchline: Lawrence's commentary — shouted through the wall as casually as if they were in the same room — establishes the specific depressing intimacy of thin-walled cheap apartment life
jokes.explanation: A good introduction to the Lawrence dynamic — the neighborly shouting-through-walls bit establishes the character and Peter's living situation efficiently. Lawrence is funny but this specific beat is primarily setup.

jokes.text: Peter: 'Damn it, Lawrence, can't you just pretend like we can't hear each other through the wall?'
jokes.setup: Lawrence has just shouted through the wall to get Peter's attention
jokes.punchline: Peter's request is for them to maintain a fiction of privacy that the walls physically cannot provide — he's asking Lawrence to pretend they have the apartment walls of adults
jokes.explanation: A good joke about the depressing informality of cheap shared-wall living. Peter's framing of it as a mutual agreement to pretend is both absurd and relatable.

jokes.text: Lawrence comes over to show Peter what he wanted him to see on channel nine: it's a cancer tumor detection segment
jokes.setup: Lawrence has urgently insisted Peter come see something on channel nine, implying it's exciting
jokes.punchline: The 'exciting thing' is a medical program about tumor detection — Lawrence's taste in television is completely miscalibrated
jokes.explanation: The misdirection works — we (and Peter) assumed 'check out this chick' on channel nine would be something entertaining or prurient, but it's a cancer screening segment. The wordless 'Aw, jeez, Lawrence' captures the deflation well.

jokes.text: Lawrence: 'Sorry, man. I thought you'd want to see this. Doesn't that chick look like Anne?'
jokes.setup: Lawrence has just shown Peter a cancer detection segment
jokes.punchline: His explanation is that the woman in the medical segment looks like Anne — connecting the tumor program to Peter's girlfriend in a way that is both clueless and oddly ominous
jokes.explanation: A good Lawrence-character joke. His reasoning is so innocent yet so wrongheaded. The implication that he was excited to show Peter because a woman on a cancer program resembled his girlfriend is a perfect character note.

jokes.text: Lawrence: 'Sometimes I get the feeling like she's cheating on me.' / Peter: 'Yeah. I get that feeling too, man.' / Peter: 'What do you mean by that?'
jokes.setup: Peter confides his suspicion about Anne; Lawrence offers apparent solidarity
jokes.punchline: This is a beat-for-beat echo of the earlier Michael Bolton moment (joke #30) — both Michael and now Lawrence seem to have specific knowledge about Anne's infidelity that they're deflecting with 'I just get that feeling'
jokes.explanation: A structural callback that deepens the Anne-cheating joke — it was funny with Michael once, and now with Lawrence it confirms a pattern. The audience realizes multiple people around Peter seem to know something he doesn't, which makes Peter's obliviousness funnier and darker.

jokes.text: Peter asks Lawrence if anyone at his construction job ever says 'Sounds like somebody's got a case of the Mondays'
jokes.setup: The waitress at Chotchkie's said 'case of the Mondays' earlier; Peter brings it to Lawrence as a point of inquiry
jokes.punchline: Lawrence's response sets up the perfect punchline — the question plants the seed before the devastating answer
jokes.explanation: The setup half of a perfect two-beat joke. Peter's research question — asking his construction-worker neighbor if 'case of the Mondays' is a universal phenomenon — implies he suspects it may be a corporate-environment-only affectation.

jokes.text: Peter asks Lawrence: 'When you come in on Monday, and you're not feelin' real well, does anyone ever say to you... Sounds like someone has a case of the Mondays?'
jokes.setup: 'Case of the Mondays' was established as an office/service industry reflex earlier; Peter brings it up with Lawrence, who works construction
jokes.punchline: Lawrence: 'No. No, man. Shit, no, man. You'd get your ass kicked, sayin' something like that, man.' — confirming the phrase exists only in a specific stratum of corporate service culture, where men cannot threaten each other with violence
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the film and a strong 8+ moment. The structure is a classic callback payoff: a phrase that was established as mildly irritating in the office context is re-evaluated through Lawrence's blue-collar lens, and the verdict is 'you'd get your ass kicked.' The comedy operates on a class-analysis level — the phrase is a symptom of a managed, liability-aware environment where real expressions of frustration are sublimated into corporate-approved chirpiness. Lawrence's response ('Shit, no, man') is both funny and reveals something true about the difference between Peter's world and his. The triple-beat 'No. No, man. Shit, no, man.' escalates beautifully. Earns its 8+ for structure, character integration, and the fact that it delivers a thematic payload while being genuinely funny.

jokes.text: Lawrence: 'Two chicks at the same time, man.' — his entire answer to 'what would you do with a million dollars'
jokes.setup: Peter has asked Lawrence what he'd do with a million dollars, in the same frame as Michael's earlier philosophical discussion about the guidance counselor exercise
jokes.punchline: Lawrence's answer is immediate, unambiguous, and entirely about sex — not wealth or freedom or experience, just 'two chicks at the same time, man'
jokes.explanation: One of the film's most quotable exchanges. Lawrence's answer is funny for its absolute clarity and lack of embarrassment — no hedging, no preamble, just 'two chicks at the same time, man.' The economy is near-perfect (seven words). The character integration is excellent: Lawrence would never give Samir's mutual-funds answer or even Michael's existential non-answer. This is Lawrence completely. Recurs later in the film (Officespace Blank Check scene) giving it additional rewatch value.

jokes.text: Lawrence's explanation: 'I think if I were a millionaire, I could hook that up, too, 'cause chicks dig dudes with money.' / Peter: 'Well, not all chicks.' / Lawrence: 'The type of chicks that would double up on a dude like me do.'
jokes.setup: Peter gently pushes back on Lawrence's two-chicks plan
jokes.punchline: Lawrence's response — 'The type of chicks that would double up on a dude like me do' — is an entirely honest and self-aware statement of his realistic dating market position, delivered without self-pity
jokes.explanation: The best line in the Lawrence sequence. 'The type of chicks that would double up on a dude like me do' is a masterpiece of honest self-assessment — Lawrence has completely internalized his own market reality and is not troubled by it in the slightest. The economy and character integration are both exceptional. This is a 9+ character-integration moment: no other character could say this line. The deadpan pragmatism is perfect.

jokes.text: Lawrence: 'You don't need a million dollars to do nothin', man. Take a look at my cousin. He's broke, don't do shit.'
jokes.setup: Peter says with a million dollars he'd do nothing — just sit on his ass
jokes.punchline: Lawrence points out that Peter's aspirational 'nothing' is already freely available — the cousin who is broke and does nothing is a living proof of concept
jokes.explanation: One of the film's best philosophical jokes and among the strongest in this reel. 'He's broke, don't do shit' demolishes the entire 'do nothing with a million dollars' fantasy in nine words by pointing out that 'nothing' is not a million-dollar lifestyle — it's freely available. The structure is perfect: setup (don't need a million), evidence (my cousin), verdict (broke, don't do shit). The economy is near-perfect. Lawrence as accidental philosopher is the richest comic vein in the film. This approaches the 8.0+ anchor quality.

jokes.text: Nina's phone loop returns during the staff meeting scene: 'Corporate accounts payable. Nina speaking. Just a moment.' — three more times in the background
jokes.setup: We cut to Initech's staff meeting with the consultant
jokes.punchline: Nina's loop is still going in the background, unchanged — a Greek chorus of corporate meaninglessness underlying Lumbergh's announcements
jokes.explanation: The return of Nina's loop serves a structural function — it anchors us back in the corporate world and signals that nothing has changed. Its power as a running gag depends on the previous iterations. Earns its keep.

jokes.text: Lumbergh introduces the consultant: '...I'd like to go ahead and welcome, uh... a new member to our team here. This is, uh... Bob Slydell.'
jokes.setup: Lumbergh is introducing the consultant at the staff meeting that has Tom in full panic
jokes.punchline: The name 'Bob Slydell' — combined with Lumbergh's signature halting, 'uh'-filled delivery — is itself a mild joke; the name sounds like a con man's alias, and Lumbergh can barely commit to even announcing it
jokes.explanation: More Lumbergh character comedy — his inability to deliver even a simple announcement without filling it with 'uh' and 'sort of' is a consistent joke. The name 'Slydell' is a running gag setup for later interactions. Functional.

jokes.text: Immediately after the consultant announcement, Lumbergh pivots to: 'Oh, and remember, next Friday is Hawaiian shirt day. So, you know, if you want to, go ahead and, uh... wear a Hawaiian shirt and jeans.'
jokes.setup: Lumbergh has just announced what amounts to a potential mass layoff via a consultant
jokes.punchline: He immediately follows the existential threat to everyone's livelihood with a note about Hawaiian shirt day — the two announcements are given identical weight in his delivery
jokes.explanation: One of the film's sharpest satirical moments. The pivot from 'we have a consultant who may fire all of you' to 'Hawaiian shirt day' — with no tonal shift whatsoever — is a perfect encapsulation of what the film is about: the corporate management class treats the existential and the trivial as equivalent, so long as the optics of casual-friendly culture are maintained. 'If you want to' adds a perfect note of hollow autonomy. This is legitimately close to an 8.5+ joke — the character integration, structure, and satirical precision are all excellent.

jokes.text: Milton's monologue: desk moved four times, used to see squirrels, they were married, Swingline vs. Boston stapler, staple retention concerns — all delivered in one unpunctuated stream of grievances to Peter
jokes.setup: Milton buttonholes Peter after the staff meeting to air grievances
jokes.punchline: The cascade of progressively more specific grievances — culminating in a precise stapler brand comparison with specific reasons for preference — creates a portrait of a man whose entire inner life is a meticulous inventory of workplace injustices
jokes.explanation: The Milton stapler monologue is one of the film's signature character moments. The escalation is masterful: each grievance is more specific than the last, culminating in the Swingline vs. Boston stapler debate, which then descends into staple storage concerns. The squirrels being 'married' is a perfect surreal detail that reveals the depth of Milton's isolation. The character integration is exceptional — this is Milton's entire psychology in one speech. The red Swingline stapler became a cultural artifact. This is a high-craft, high-impact moment.

jokes.text: Milton: 'I'll set the building on fire.'
jokes.setup: Milton has been building his list of workplace injustices; the stapler is the final indignity
jokes.punchline: His threat to burn the building down is delivered in exactly the same flat, bureaucratic tone as his complaint about the stapler — no escalation, no menace, just a matter-of-fact statement of intent
jokes.explanation: The best single joke in this reel and one of the best moments in the film. 'I'll set the building on fire' is a perfect comedic line for multiple reasons: (1) it's delivered in exactly the same tone as every other Milton grievance — the absence of escalation is the entire joke; (2) it pays off the entire Milton introduction (the radio negotiation, the stapler obsession) in a single line; (3) it foreshadows the film's climax literally and exactly; (4) the phrase itself is both specific and final. The craft components are all near-maximum — it's original, structurally perfect, could ONLY be this character, maximally economical, and completely earned by everything preceding it. This is comparable to or exceeding the Snip-Snap anchor in terms of character-integrated comedic precision.

jokes.text: Peter: 'OK, well, that sounds great. Uh, I'll talk to you later, all right? Bye.' — responding to 'I'll set the building on fire' as if Milton said something perfectly normal
jokes.setup: Milton has just threatened to commit arson
jokes.punchline: Peter's response — 'OK, well, that sounds great' — treats the arson threat as a satisfactory conclusion to a mundane conversation and ends it with cheerful corporate pleasantry
jokes.explanation: The perfect reaction to Milton's arson threat. 'OK, well, that sounds great' — using Lumbergh's own verbal tic ('that would be great') in response to an arson threat — is a callback that doubles as character revelation: Peter has been so beaten down by corporate pleasantry that he now deploys it to dismiss genuine threats. The economy is exceptional and the structure (arson / 'that sounds great' / 'talk to you later, all right? Bye') is flawless. This is an 8+ reaction beat.

jokes.text: Bill Lumbergh asking Peter to come in on Saturday AND Sunday, delivered in his signature passive-aggressive, meandering corporate-speak
jokes.setup: Bill opens with the already-established Saturday ask, which we know Peter hates
jokes.punchline: He casually adds Sunday too, buried in corporate throat-clearing filler ('Oh, oh, and I almost forgot... we lost some people this week')
jokes.explanation: Lumbergh's verbal tics ('go ahead and', 'that would be great', 'OK?') are peak character comedy — no one else in cinema delivers workplace passive-aggression this precisely. The escalation from Saturday to Sunday lands because the audience has already been primed to dread this character's requests.

jokes.text: Peter's confession: 'every single day of my life has been worse than the day before it. So that means that every single day that you see me, that's on the worst day of my life.'
jokes.setup: Peter is in what appears to be a therapy session, beginning to describe his work life
jokes.punchline: The logical syllogism he delivers — stated completely earnestly — means TODAY is statistically his worst day ever, every day, forever
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the reel and one of the best in the film. The formal logical structure ('that means that every single day...') gives a genuinely bleak insight the shape of a proof theorem. It's dark, it's precise, it's perfectly delivered as deadpan sincerity. The punchline isn't a twist — it's the conclusion of his own ironclad logic, which makes it both funnier and sadder. Highly quotable and culturally resonant for anyone who has worked a soul-crushing job.

jokes.text: Therapist: 'What about today? Is today the worst day of your life?' Peter: 'Yeah.' Therapist: 'Wow. That's messed up.'
jokes.setup: Peter has just delivered his devastating life-worsening theorem
jokes.punchline: The therapist's completely unprofessional, colloquial response — 'Wow. That's messed up.' — is the opposite of therapeutic framing
jokes.explanation: The economy here is extraordinary — four words ('That's messed up') destroy all professional pretense and validate Peter's despair in the most un-therapist way possible. The comedic surprise is that the therapist confirms rather than reframes the problem. Perfect straight-man subversion.

jokes.text: Peter asks the therapist if he can be hypnotized so he doesn't know he's at work — 'Could I come home and think that I've been fishing all day or something?'
jokes.setup: Peter is seeking therapy for work-related misery
jokes.punchline: His proposed solution — total dissociation from reality, specifically fishing as the fantasy — is completely earnest and utterly unhinged as a therapeutic request
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'fishing' makes this. Peter's brain goes to the most pastoral, low-stakes activity imaginable as the antidote to software engineering. The deadpan delivery of a genuinely insane therapeutic request — presented as reasonable — is very much Peter's character voice.

jokes.text: Dr. Swanson dies mid-hypnosis, leaving Peter permanently hypnotized into a state of total relaxation
jokes.setup: Dr. Swanson is guiding Peter into deep hypnotic relaxation, counting down from three
jokes.punchline: The doctor's labored breathing and sudden collapse (and Anne's scream) reveal he has died before snapping Peter out — leaving Peter in a permanent blissful state
jokes.explanation: This is brilliantly constructed dark comedy. The hypnosis scene is played completely straight, the doctor's voice slowing and laboring in a way that retroactively recontextualizes the whole session. The punchline — that Peter's transformation into a care-free person comes from a man literally dying — is both hilarious and structurally elegant. It's the film's inciting incident delivered as black comedy. The setup is meticulous and the payoff is completely earned.

jokes.text: Anne's panicked 'Where's the phone? Where's the goddamn phone?!' while Peter sits blissfully unresponsive
jokes.setup: Dr. Swanson has collapsed; chaos erupts around Peter
jokes.punchline: Peter, still hypnotized into complete relaxation, sits inert in his chair while everyone panics around him — the juxtaposition of his serenity against the emergency is the joke
jokes.explanation: The visual comedy here is Peter as a serene island in a sea of panic. Anne's frantic, profane scramble for the phone ('the goddamn phone') while Peter does nothing plays as both cringe and visual gag. The specificity of her panic — she can't even find the phone — adds to the chaos.

jokes.text: Cut to Peter contentedly lounging at home, phone ringing — Lumbergh has left multiple answering machine messages about Peter not showing up
jokes.setup: We know Peter is now hypnotized into not caring; Lumbergh has been calling
jokes.punchline: Peter is blissfully home doing nothing while Lumbergh's voice drones passive-aggressively on the machine — the exact scenario Peter fantasized about (not being mentally at work)
jokes.explanation: The irony is exquisite — Peter asked to be mentally removed from work, and now Lumbergh's voice is literally in his home and Peter simply doesn't care. The intercutting of Lumbergh's escalating machine messages with Peter's complete peace is a structurally satisfying payoff.

jokes.text: Lumbergh's first voicemail: 'Yeah, hi, it's Bill Lumbergh. It's about ten o'clock. Yeah. Just, uh, wondering where you are.'
jokes.setup: Peter is absent; Lumbergh expected him in
jokes.punchline: Lumbergh's voicemail is as performatively casual and agonizingly hedged as his in-person speech — 'just, uh, wondering where you are' as if it's nothing
jokes.explanation: Lumbergh's voice is a comedic instrument in itself. The voicemail format perfectly captures his brand of passive-aggressive management — the performative casualness of 'just wondering where you are' when he is clearly furious. Very high character integration because this only works with Lumbergh's specific speech tics.

jokes.text: Lumbergh's answering machine messages escalating from polite to multiple callbacks: 'Yeah. Hi. It's Bill Lum-- Yeah. It's-- Yeah. Hi. It's Bill Lumber--'
jokes.setup: Lumbergh has already left two professional messages; this is apparently another attempt
jokes.punchline: He can't even complete his own name — the machine keeps cutting him off or he's flustered — turning his corporate composure into comic fragmentation
jokes.explanation: Lumbergh's verbal tic of labored filler phrases ('Yeah. Hi.') becoming a stutter when he's slightly off-script is a perfect extension of his character. The joke is that his composure only works when he's in control — the machine, a simple technology, undoes him.

jokes.text: Anne calls Peter at home at 3:30pm asking why he's not at work; Peter says 'Because I-- I didn't feel like it.'
jokes.setup: Anne (Peter's girlfriend) calls, alarmed he's not at work
jokes.punchline: 'I didn't feel like it' — delivered with no defensiveness, complete honesty, as if this is a totally reasonable explanation for skipping work
jokes.explanation: The economy of 'I didn't feel like it' as an answer to 'why aren't you at work' is devastating in its simplicity. Post-hypnosis Peter has achieved what every office worker fantasizes — the ability to simply opt out with zero social anxiety. It's delivered as the most natural thing in the world, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Anne's indictment list: Peter sat there while Dr. Swanson died, then walked out embarrassing her in front of friends — delivered as grievances equal in weight
jokes.setup: Anne is confronting Peter about his behavior
jokes.punchline: She lists 'just sat there while Dr. Swanson DIES' and 'embarrassed me in front of my friends' as equivalent complaints, as if social embarrassment and witnessing a death are morally comparable grievances
jokes.explanation: The comedy comes from Anne's moral hierarchy — a man's death is listed as a problem primarily because of what it meant for her social standing. It characterizes her as self-absorbed while also being darkly funny about how people process trauma.

jokes.text: Anne's breakup message escalates to: 'Oh, and one more thing — I've been cheating on you!' delivered as an afterthought kicker
jokes.setup: Anne calls back furious that Peter hung up on her, declares they're through
jokes.punchline: 'Oh, and one more thing — I've been cheating on you!' dropped as a casual postscript, like remembering to mention she forgot to pick up milk
jokes.explanation: The 'one more thing' construction perfectly mimics the rhythm of an afterthought — something trivial you almost forgot. Using that structure for a confession of infidelity is a sharp inversion. The fact that Peter, still blissed out, presumably doesn't care makes it even richer (implied by context). Clean, well-structured punchline.

jokes.text: Cut to Lumbergh's meeting about TPS time sheets — Tom asks 'Where's Peter?' in the middle of Lumbergh droning on
jokes.setup: Lumbergh is delivering a tedious time-sheet policy update; Peter is conspicuously absent
jokes.punchline: Tom's aside ('Where's Peter? I heard he didn't show up this weekend') punctures the meeting's banality and implicitly contrasts with what we know Peter is doing (nothing, blissfully)
jokes.explanation: Functional transitional joke — the contrast between the boring meeting and Peter's absence does work, and 'Who's that guy?' from Michael about an unnamed co-worker adds a small absurdist beat. Not particularly crafted but serves its purpose.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Who's that guy?' — apparently not knowing a coworker who attends the same meeting
jokes.setup: Tom asks about Peter; there's apparently another person at the meeting
jokes.punchline: Michael genuinely doesn't know who a person in his own office meeting is — suggesting the dehumanizing anonymity of corporate life has reached pure absurdism
jokes.explanation: Brief but lands a small absurdist point about how interchangeable office workers are to each other. The economy is good — three words do the job. Not a standout but a solid throwaway.

jokes.text: Brian the waiter's enthusiastic 'Hey, look who's back!' when Peter walks into Chotchkie's
jokes.setup: Peter has walked into the restaurant where Joanna works, apparently mid-week during work hours
jokes.punchline: Brian's over-enthusiastic greeting underscores that Peter, a software engineer, is apparently a regular enough at a chain restaurant that the staff recognizes him
jokes.explanation: Minor joke that establishes the setting and Peter's regular-customer status. Functions as a bridge more than a standalone laugh, but Brian's exaggerated cheerfulness is a small character note.

jokes.text: Peter asks Joanna to lunch while she's actively trying to tell him the daily specials — 'It's actually right there on the board. Excuse me.'
jokes.setup: Peter asks 'what are you doing for lunch' — Joanna assumes it's a customer asking about specials
jokes.punchline: She goes into server-mode and points to the board before realizing he's asking her personally, creating a moment of crossed intentions
jokes.explanation: Nicely observed moment of ambiguous communication — the server/customer dynamic vs. the personal ask. Joanna defaulting to 'it's on the board' is both realistic and a small character reveal about how she's conditioned by her job.

jokes.text: Peter's smooth exit strategy: 'I'm gonna go next door and get a table, and if you'd like to join me, no big deal... And if not, that's cool, too.'
jokes.setup: Joanna is hesitant about breaking the rule against lunch with customers
jokes.punchline: Peter's casually unattached offer — the hypnosis-induced total lack of anxiety — is the antithesis of how nervous people normally ask someone out, and it's absurdly effective
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels: it's genuinely good pickup advice (non-needy confidence), it characterizes Peter's post-hypnosis state, and it contrasts with how desperate and anxious Peter presumably would have been before. The 'that's cool, too' is the punchline — the total indifference only someone in a hypnotic state of relaxation could authentically pull off.

jokes.text: Tom Smykowski's interview: consultants ask what he does and he explains he takes specs from customers to engineers — then admits his secretary does it, or the fax
jokes.setup: Tom confidently explains his liaison role between customers and engineers
jokes.punchline: Layer by layer, the consultants strip away every actual task he describes until it's clear he does nothing — 'Well, no. My secretary does that. Or the fax.'
jokes.explanation: Brilliantly structured cringe comedy. The Bobs conduct a Socratic demolition of Tom's job description in real time, each follow-up question collapsing one more pillar of his self-justification. 'Well, no. I mean... sometimes.' is the perfect deflation. The escalating structure builds to the knockout 'What would you say you do here?' The comedy is rooted in a universal workplace truth: many middle-management roles exist to justify themselves.

jokes.text: 'I deal with the goddamn customers so the engineers don't have to! I have people skills! I am good at dealing with people! Can't you understand that?! What the hell is wrong with you people?!'
jokes.setup: The Bobs have methodically exposed that Tom does nothing concrete; Tom is now cornered
jokes.punchline: Tom's complete meltdown — screaming 'I HAVE PEOPLE SKILLS' while demonstrating catastrophically bad people skills — is the ultimate ironic self-own
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable moments in the film and a perfect example of comedy through ironic self-contradiction. Tom claiming 'people skills' while screaming at the people he's supposed to be skilled with is a flawless comedic construction. It escalates naturally from the Bobs' interrogation (#19), arrives at exactly the right moment of maximum pressure, and the specific phrasing ('I AM GOOD AT DEALING WITH PEOPLE!') is both hilarious and painfully true to the character type. This is at the level of the anchor examples — broadly quotable, culturally resonant, structurally perfect.

jokes.text: Bobs discover Michael's name is 'Michael Bolton' — 'Are you any relation to the pop singer?'
jokes.setup: The Bobs are interviewing Michael; they read his name from a list
jokes.punchline: The name turns out to be the same as the famous pop singer, triggering the Bobs' unironic enthusiasm for Michael Bolton's music
jokes.explanation: This joke works on three levels simultaneously: the humiliation of sharing a name with an uncool pop singer, the Bobs' sincere enthusiasm for said singer (characterizing them as middle-management square types), and Michael's trapped politeness in having to agree that Michael Bolton is 'pretty good.' The setup (established elsewhere in the film) pays off beautifully here.

jokes.text: Bob Slydell: 'For my money, I don't know if it gets any better than when he sings "When a Man Loves a Woman."' — delivered with genuine, embarrassing sincerity
jokes.setup: The Bobs have established they're Michael Bolton fans
jokes.punchline: Slydell's specific, earnest enthusiasm for a notoriously schlocky song — sung with complete conviction — is the most embarrassing possible endorsement
jokes.explanation: The joke is in Slydell's specificity and sincerity — this isn't mocking Michael Bolton for laughs, it's using the Bobs' genuine taste as a character indictment. Men who make corporate layoff decisions in dead-eyed meetings love 'When a Man Loves a Woman.' The comedy is observational and character-driven.

jokes.text: Michael is forced to admit he likes all of Michael Bolton's songs when Bobs ask his favorite — 'I guess I sort of like them all.'
jokes.setup: The Bobs have enthusiastically pushed Michael to confess his Bolton preference
jokes.punchline: Michael, deeply humiliated, can't name a song without fully endorsing his namesake — 'I guess I sort of like them all' is maximum capitulation
jokes.explanation: The escalating social trap is exquisitely designed. Michael can't reject Bolton without seeming weird (why hate the guy just for the name?) and can't embrace him without humiliation. His tortured non-answer 'I sort of like them all' is the only escape hatch, and it's perfectly pathetic. 'I celebrate the guy's entire catalog' from Slydell then twists the knife.

jokes.text: Slydell: 'I celebrate the guy's entire catalog.' Then: 'Anyway, let's get down to business, Michael.' Michael: 'You can just call me Mike.'
jokes.setup: Slydell has just delivered his most effusive Bolton endorsement
jokes.punchline: Michael's desperate attempt to distance himself from his name — 'You can just call me Mike' — is the logical conclusion of his entire predicament, and the pivot from catalog celebration to business is jarring and funny
jokes.explanation: The 'call me Mike' button is the perfect capper to the Bolton sequence. It arrives at exactly the right moment, is completely in character (Michael hates his name throughout the film), and the economy is surgical — two words deflate the entire preceding agony. Slydell's oblivious pivot back to business as if none of that just happened adds a final layer.

jokes.text: Peter asks 'I wonder if I'm allowed to wear this in here?' about some item of clothing — at Flinger's, a competitor to his girlfriend's restaurant
jokes.setup: Peter and Joanna are sitting down at Flinger's; Peter is apparently wearing something associated with Chotchkie's or his workplace
jokes.punchline: The anxiety about workplace dress codes extending to a casual lunch — or possibly wearing a competing restaurant's gear — is a small but pointed joke about how corporate culture colonizes personal life
jokes.explanation: Minor observational beat — the humor comes from the implicit nervousness about dress-code rules even in a personal, non-work context. Functions as scene-setting more than a sharp joke.

jokes.text: Joanna: 'Wow! This place is really nice. Yeah, my God, compared to Chotchkie's!'
jokes.setup: They're sitting at Flinger's, an obviously identical chain restaurant to Chotchkie's
jokes.punchline: Joanna is genuinely impressed by what is visibly an equally mediocre chain restaurant — her standards have been so lowered by Chotchkie's that Flinger's reads as luxury
jokes.explanation: Lands nicely as a payoff to the 'Chili's or Flinger's' joke — the film has established these places are interchangeable, so Joanna's sincere admiration of Flinger's over Chotchkie's is a soft absurdist joke. Character-revealing too: her job has that thoroughly ground down.

jokes.text: Peter notices something on Joanna's suspenders — 'We're not in Kansas anymore' button — leading to the revelation about 'flair'
jokes.setup: Peter notices Joanna's 'flair' buttons and asks about them
jokes.punchline: The concept of 'flair' — mandatory fun expressed through 15 required pieces of corporate-mandated personality — is itself the joke, delivered through Joanna's embarrassed explanation
jokes.explanation: The 'flair' concept is one of the film's most enduring satirical inventions — institutionalized forced personality expression that is by definition not personal. Joanna's shame about it ('I don't even know what they say. I don't really care.') is both funny and sad. The concept has become a cultural shorthand for mandatory corporate cheerfulness.

jokes.text: Joanna: 'I don't even know what they say. I don't really care. I don't really like talking about my flair.'
jokes.setup: Peter has asked if she chose her flair herself
jokes.punchline: Joanna's complete disengagement from her own mandatory self-expression — she 'just grabbed fifteen buttons' and doesn't even know what they say — is the perfect encapsulation of the film's thesis about corporate dehumanization
jokes.explanation: The comedy deepens on the flair concept: the whole point of flair is 'personality,' and Joanna's total alienation from her own flair pins the satire perfectly. She wore it for so long she forgot what it said. This is both a laugh line and a quietly devastating character moment.

jokes.text: Peter explains the Y2K bug to Joanna, trails off mid-sentence with '...It doesn't really matter. I don't like my job, and I don't think I'm gonna go anymore.'
jokes.setup: Peter is explaining what he does at Initiech — the Y2K software fix
jokes.punchline: He literally stops explaining mid-sentence, decides it doesn't matter, and announces with zero drama that he's quitting by simply never going back
jokes.explanation: One of the most perfectly constructed lines of the film. The Y2K explanation trails off — not because Peter can't explain it, but because even explaining his pointless job feels pointless. Then: 'I don't think I'm gonna go anymore.' No drama, no buildup, stated as a simple preference. The hypnosis has freed him to say out loud what every office worker thinks but never voices. The line sits at the intersection of dark comedy and genuine liberation fantasy, and it's completely character-specific.

jokes.text: Joanna: 'So you're gonna quit?' Peter: 'Nah-uh. Not really. I'm just gonna stop going.'
jokes.setup: Joanna tries to categorize Peter's decision in normal terms ('so you're gonna quit?')
jokes.punchline: Peter distinguishes between 'quitting' (formal, decisive) and 'just stopping going' (passive, no confrontation) — the distinction is both meaningless and hilarious
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic logic: quitting implies confrontation, paperwork, formal process — but Peter has achieved a state beyond caring enough to even quit. 'I'm just gonna stop going' is both deeply funny and a genuinely distinct philosophical position. The distinction between quitting and simply not showing up is a hairline crack that opens into an absurd chasm. Highly quotable and deeply character-specific to post-hypnosis Peter.

jokes.text: Peter: 'You know, I've never really liked paying bills. I don't think I'm gonna do that, either.'
jokes.setup: Joanna asks what he'll do about money and bills
jokes.punchline: Peter applies the same logic to bills as he did to work — if he doesn't like it, he won't do it — escalating his philosophy of radical indifference to financial reality
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Peter's new worldview from 'not going to work' to 'not paying bills' either maintains perfect comic logic (he applies the same framework universally) or exposes its absurdity — and both readings are funny. The economy is exceptional: 'I've never really liked paying bills' mirrors the structure of his job statement exactly. This is running-gag escalation at its best.

jokes.text: Peter: 'I want to take you out to dinner and then I want to go back to my apartment and watch Kung Fu. Do you ever watch Kung Fu? I love Kung Fu. Channel 39.'
jokes.setup: Joanna asks what Peter actually wants to do with his life
jokes.punchline: His complete answer: dinner, then 'Kung Fu' on channel 39 — a stunningly unpretentious and specific vision of contentment that is both funny and oddly charming
jokes.explanation: The 'Channel 39' specificity is what makes this. Peter isn't fantasizing about travel, wealth, or adventure — he wants Kung Fu reruns on the right channel. This is both a character reveal and a gentle absurdist joke about how modest true contentment can be. The delivery — 'I love Kung Fu. Channel 39.' — is straight-faced and sincere, which elevates it.

jokes.text: Bill Lumbergh apparently just took someone's stapler during a conversation — audible laughter from the room before he hangs up the phone
jokes.setup: Lumbergh is on the phone in his office
jokes.punchline: The snippet of overheard conversation — '...took a stapler off my desk...' followed by laughter — implies Lumbergh is either recounting or perpetuating another stapler confiscation, a callback to Milton's stapler subplot
jokes.explanation: A blink-and-miss-it callback that rewards attentive viewers. The snippet is intentionally incomplete — we don't get the full context — which makes it funnier as an overheard fragment. Lumbergh casually discussing stapler confiscation as business-as-usual is very much in character.

jokes.text: Lumbergh makes Milton move his desk again — 'as far back against that wall as possible' — and takes his stapler mid-conversation with zero acknowledgment of Milton's objection
jokes.setup: Lumbergh approaches Milton at his desk with his signature passive corporate voice
jokes.punchline: He casually grabs Milton's stapler while delivering desk-move instructions, treating Milton's protest ('No, because I was--') as literally nothing, completing the interaction with 'Thanks a bunch, Milton. Good-bye.'
jokes.explanation: This is Lumbergh and Milton at their peak — the interaction is a clinic in power-imbalance comedy. Lumbergh's obliviousness to Milton as a human being is total: he takes the stapler mid-sentence, talks over Milton's objection, and signs off with 'Thanks a bunch.' The comedy is in the absolute asymmetry of acknowledgment. 'Thanks a bunch' as a closing line after casual theft is the perfect button.

jokes.text: Milton, alone after Lumbergh leaves: 'I could set the building on fire.'
jokes.setup: Milton has just been robbed of his stapler and ordered to move his desk again, muttering throughout
jokes.punchline: His quiet, matter-of-fact arson threat — not shouted, not dramatic, just mumbled as a reasonable option — is both hilarious and ominous
jokes.explanation: One of the great comic lines in American cinema, and it earns every superlative. The power is in what it doesn't do: Milton doesn't rage, doesn't explode, doesn't even raise his voice. He mutters 'I could set the building on fire' the way you'd say 'I could make a sandwich.' The deadpan delivery of a catastrophic threat makes it both funnier and genuinely unnerving. It's purely character-specific — only Milton could deliver this line this way. And (for rewatchers) it plants the film's climax. Perfect economy, perfect character integration, perfect dark subversive tone.

jokes.text: Michael's reaction to seeing Peter walk into Initiech: 'I thought you'd come in here and start shooting.'
jokes.setup: Peter unexpectedly shows up at the office after a weekend AWOL
jokes.punchline: Michael's immediate assumption — not 'you got fired' or 'you're in trouble' but 'I thought you'd start shooting' — reveals how thoroughly the office has normalized workplace violence as a logical response to their conditions
jokes.explanation: Dark joke that lands because it's delivered as a completely reasonable, even sympathetic assumption. Michael isn't alarmed — he's almost concerned he was wrong. The normalization of extreme responses to workplace misery is very much in Office Space's wheelhouse.

jokes.text: Peter: 'Michael, I did nothing. I did absolutely nothing, and it was everything that I thought it could be.'
jokes.setup: Michael demands to know what Peter was doing all weekend instead of coming into work
jokes.punchline: Peter's response reframes 'doing nothing' as a positive achievement — 'everything that I thought it could be' — with the earnest satisfaction of someone who has climbed Everest
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable lines in the film and a thesis statement for the whole movie. 'It was everything that I thought it could be' applied to doing nothing is a perfect inversion of achievement rhetoric — the language of ambition deployed for radical inaction. The structure is immaculate: setup ('I did nothing'), restatement ('I did absolutely nothing'), then the payoff phrasing. Character-specific to post-hypnosis Peter and deeply resonant for anyone who has fantasized about opting out.

jokes.text: Peter: 'Michael, I did nothing. I did absolutely nothing, and it was everything that I thought it could be.'
jokes.setup: Michael asks what Peter was doing instead of coming to work
jokes.punchline: 'I did absolutely nothing, and it was everything that I thought it could be' — a perfect inversion of achievement rhetoric applied to doing nothing
jokes.explanation: Exceptional line. 'Everything that I thought it could be' is the language of dreams and ambitions applied to inactivity — a complete comedic inversion of hustle culture. The parallel structure ('I did nothing... I did absolutely nothing') builds perfectly to the payoff. This is a quotable, deeply resonant joke that captures something true about the dream of pure leisure. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor and exceeds it in my view.

jokes.text: Bob Slydell: 'Ah, there you are. We were just talking about you. You must be Peter Gibbons.' Peter: 'Uh-huh. Terrific.'
jokes.setup: Peter wanders into his consultant interview without anxiety, preparation, or apparent concern
jokes.punchline: 'Uh-huh. Terrific.' — Peter's response to being greeted and identified, delivered with the enthusiasm of someone confirming a coffee order
jokes.explanation: Minor but pointed. Peter's 'Uh-huh. Terrific.' in response to being greeted by the people who will decide his employment fate is a perfect capsule of his current state. The word 'terrific' is Lumbergh's word — its reappropriation by a checked-out Peter gives it a slight added layer.

jokes.text: Peter: 'I'd say in a given week I probably only do about fifteen minutes of real, actual work.'
jokes.setup: Peter has described late arrival, side door avoidance, staring at desk — the culmination of his honest accounting
jokes.punchline: The final tally: fifteen minutes of actual work per week — delivered as a sincere estimate, not a boast
jokes.explanation: The punchline number — fifteen minutes — is perfect. Not zero (that would be absurd) and not an hour (that would be underwhelming). Fifteen minutes is specific enough to be funny and low enough to be shocking. The specificity of 'real, actual work' (as opposed to all the fake work already described) is a great qualifier. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Peter: 'I'd say in a given week, I probably only do about fifteen minutes of real, actual work.'
jokes.setup: Peter is building on his workplace confession to the Bobs
jokes.punchline: The specific quantification — 'fifteen minutes' in a 40-hour week — delivered as a completely honest assessment, is both absurd and uncomfortably relatable
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'fifteen minutes' is key — not 'a little' or 'hardly any' but fifteen. It's exact enough to feel true and small enough to be scandalous. The qualifier 'real, actual work' implies he has thought carefully about what qualifies. This is the kind of office truth that lands with audiences because it articulates something universally felt but never said.

jokes.text: Peter's TPS report confession: 'The thing is, Bob, it's not that I'm lazy. It's that I just don't care.'
jokes.setup: Bobs invite Peter to tell them more; he begins explaining TPS reports
jokes.punchline: The distinction between 'lazy' and 'not caring' — presented with philosophical precision — reframes his behavior not as a character flaw but as a rational response to a pointless system
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable lines in the film and a philosophical pivot point. 'It's not that I'm lazy, it's that I just don't care' is a genuinely sophisticated distinction — laziness implies wanting to avoid effort; not caring means the system itself has lost legitimacy. The Bobs' follow-up 'Don't... don't care?' shows they've never encountered this framing. Delivered with total calm, it hits harder than any rant could.

jokes.text: Peter's motivation speech: 'I have eight different bosses right now... when I make a mistake, I have eight different people coming by to tell me about it.'
jokes.setup: Peter is explaining why he lacks motivation at work
jokes.punchline: The repetition of 'eight' — 'eight bosses,' 'eight different people' — hammered three times in quick succession, makes the absurdity concrete and the indignation rhythmically funny
jokes.explanation: The 'eight bosses' speech is a masterclass in comic rhythm. The word 'eight' repeated insistently — 'Eight bosses. Eight? Eight, Bob.' — makes the exchange feel like a riff. The diagnosis (I only get negative feedback, never positive) is acutely observed corporate dysfunction, and Peter's calm delivery of a genuinely outrageous workplace situation is very effective.

jokes.text: Peter: 'That's my only real motivation, is not to be hassled. That and the fear of losing my job. But you know, Bob, that'll only make someone work just hard enough not to get fired.'
jokes.setup: Peter has explained his demotivation; now he describes the actual motivators he does have
jokes.punchline: The honest description of negative-only motivation — 'just hard enough not to get fired' — is a devastating management indictment delivered as simple logic, not complaint
jokes.explanation: This is Mike Judge at his most acute. 'Just hard enough not to get fired' is not just funny — it's a perfect articulation of how negative-reinforcement management actually works in practice. The line has a prophetic, aphoristic quality. The fact that Peter delivers it not as a complaint but as a logical observation makes it both funnier and more damning.

jokes.text: Peter: 'Good luck with your layoffs, all right? I hope your firings go really well.'
jokes.setup: Peter ends his interview and is walking out
jokes.punchline: He wishes the Bobs good luck with 'your layoffs' — treating their consultancy work as something to be cheerfully wished well, like wishing someone luck on a golf game
jokes.explanation: Brilliant social transgression. 'Good luck with your layoffs, all right? I hope your firings go really well' treats the destruction of people's livelihoods as a neutral professional task deserving of well-wishes. Peter's sincerity is what makes it land — he's not being snide, he genuinely means it. The Bobs' bewildered-then-charmed reaction ('Great. Wow.') confirms the joke's effectiveness. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Bill Lumbergh intercepts Peter immediately after the interview — 'So, Peter, what's happening?' — the most dreaded voice at the most inopportune moment
jokes.setup: Peter has just had the most transgressive work interview imaginable and is walking out on a high
jokes.punchline: Lumbergh's 'So, Peter, what's happening?' — his signature opener — lands as a puncture of the moment, the institutional system reasserting itself
jokes.explanation: The running gag of Lumbergh's 'What's happening?' is well-deployed here — it arrives at the moment Peter is most liberated, reasserting the mundane institutional world. The cut away before Peter responds adds to the joke (we don't need to hear Peter's answer; the interruption itself is the punchline).

jokes.text: Stan: 'Well, like Brian, for example, has thirty-seven pieces of flair on today. And a terrific smile.'
jokes.setup: Stan is making the case that Joanna should wear more flair
jokes.punchline: 'And a terrific smile' — tacked on as a separate achievement, as if smiling is a quantifiable workplace KPI alongside flair count
jokes.explanation: The 'terrific smile' addendum is a perfect comic beat. Stan has listed a smile as a discrete, comparable metric — 37 flair AND a smile — which captures how deranged corporate enthusiasm culture is. The specificity of '37' vs '15' is also good: it's not 20 or 25 but 37, which feels both precise and arbitrary.

jokes.text: Stan's flair speech: 'People can get a cheeseburger anywhere, OK? They come to Chotchkie's for the atmosphere and the attitude. That's what the flair's about. It's about fun.'
jokes.setup: Stan is trying to explain the deeper corporate philosophy of flair to a visibly uncomfortable Joanna
jokes.punchline: 'It's about fun' — delivered with managerial gravity about mandatory button-wearing — is the satire's thesis in miniature: forced fun is the opposite of fun
jokes.explanation: Stan is a terrific corporate-speak caricature and this is his best speech. The earnest delivery of 'it's about fun' about a mandatory dress code is the whole movie's thesis in one sentence. The logic — people come for atmosphere, the flair creates atmosphere, therefore flair = fun — is exactly how corporate culture justifies mandates as freedom. Well-crafted satire that is funny AND insightful.

jokes.text: Stan: 'Look, we want you to express yourself, OK? ...Now if you feel that the bare minimum is enough, then OK, but some people choose to wear more and we encourage that, OK? You do want to express yourself, don't you?'
jokes.setup: Stan has just said flair is about self-expression and fun
jokes.punchline: He then guilt-trips Joanna into more flair with 'You DO want to express yourself, don't you?' — using the language of self-expression to coerce compliance, with a passive-aggressive implied 'or are you a bad employee?'
jokes.explanation: This is the sharpest moment in the flair sequence. 'You DO want to express yourself, don't you?' is a rhetorical trap — say no and you're suppressing yourself, say yes and you'll wear more flair. It captures perfectly how corporate culture uses the language of autonomy and self-expression to enforce conformity. The cringe is exquisite: Stan isn't a villain, he genuinely believes what he's saying, which makes it worse. This is craft-level satire.

jokes.text: Bobs' meeting: 'Then there's Tom Smykowski. He's useless. Gone.'
jokes.setup: Bobs are going through the Initiech staff list with management, recommending layoffs
jokes.punchline: 'He's useless. Gone.' — the same Tom who just had a full nervous breakdown explaining his job is dispatched in two words with zero ceremony
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic payoff to Tom's 'I HAVE PEOPLE SKILLS' meltdown. Everything he said and did — the full emotional spectacle — is condensed by the Bobs into 'He's useless. Gone.' The brutality is funny precisely because it's so efficient and so accurate. The economy is flawless.

jokes.text: Milton Waddams revelation: he was laid off five years ago and no one told him — he's still been getting paychecks due to a payroll glitch
jokes.setup: Bobs are discussing Milton, whom no one can place as a current employee
jokes.punchline: Milton was laid off five years ago, never informed, and has been a ghost employee collecting paychecks ever since — the company's bureaucracy was so dysfunctional it couldn't even execute a layoff
jokes.explanation: This revelation recontextualizes everything about Milton — the desk-moving, the stapler, the mumbled threats — as the company's unconscious cruelty toward a man they technically already fired.
