The absurdity is rich and deeply dark: corporate bureaucracy is so broken it accidentally retained a laid-off employee for five years. This is the film's best structural setup for future payoff.

jokes.text: Bob Slydell: 'We fixed the glitch. So he won't be receiving a paycheck anymore. So it'll just work itself out naturally.'
jokes.setup: Dom asks if Milton has been 'let go'; Slydell corrects him
jokes.punchline: 'We fixed the glitch' — no conversation, no severance, no acknowledgment of the five-year oversight — Milton's income will simply stop. 'It'll just work itself out naturally.' The euphemism for letting a man unknowingly starve.
jokes.explanation: This is some of Mike Judge's darkest and most precise writing. 'We fixed the glitch' reduces a human being's livelihood to a software bug. 'It'll just work itself out naturally' is a grotesque euphemism for letting Milton's situation deteriorate until he notices he has no income. The Bobs' preference for 'avoid confrontation whenever possible' applied to human management is both funny and chilling. Perfect corporate-speak satire, and Porter's 'We always like to avoid confrontation whenever possible' adds an extra layer of institutional cowardice dressed as policy.

jokes.text: Porter: 'We always like to avoid confrontation whenever possible.'
jokes.setup: The Bobs have just explained they will silently stop Milton's pay and wait for him to disappear
jokes.punchline: Porter offers 'we always like to avoid confrontation' as the justification — a corporate value used to justify something genuinely cruel and cowardly
jokes.explanation: Perfect encapsulation of corporate conflict-avoidance culture. 'We like to avoid confrontation' is an actual value statement in many corporate cultures, here applied to its logical extreme: avoiding confrontation so thoroughly that you'd rather passive-aggressively starve someone out than have a conversation. The deadpan delivery makes it a genuinely great satirical line.

jokes.text: Bobs recommend Peter Gibbons for upper management: 'That's just a straight shooter with upper management written all over him.'
jokes.setup: The Bobs have just seen Peter's interview — during which he admitted to doing 15 minutes of work per week and not caring at all
jokes.punchline: The Bobs loved it. Peter's total honesty read as executive presence. 'Upper management written all over him.'
jokes.explanation: The satirical reversal is exquisite: the film has just spent several minutes letting Peter destroy himself in an interview, and the Bobs' verdict is that he's exactly what management looks like. The implication — that executive ranks are full of people who don't care and don't work — is delivered not as a rant but as a cheerful evaluation. Perfectly constructed, devastating satire.

jokes.text: Bobs praising Peter to management: 'That's just a straight shooter with upper management written all over him.'
jokes.setup: The Bobs are reviewing Peter's interview — which the audience knows was a confession of minimal work and total disengagement
jokes.punchline: The consultants loved Peter's honesty and want to promote him — a complete inversion of what any rational manager would conclude from Peter's answers
jokes.explanation: The twist that Peter's radical honesty impresses the consultants is a brilliantly structured payoff. It works on multiple levels: it validates Peter's new hypnosis-induced worldview, it satirizes management consulting (which values 'authenticity' as a trait), and it sets up the entire second half of the film. 'Straight shooter with upper management written all over him' is a funny corporate phrase applied to the least corporate person in the building. Strong ironic reversal.

jokes.text: Lumbergh immediately tries to undercut Peter's recommendation: 'He's been real flaky lately... and he's been having some problems with his T.P.S. reports.'
jokes.setup: Bobs have enthusiastically recommended Peter for upper management
jokes.punchline: Lumbergh's objections — 'flaky' and 'TPS reports' — are both petty and revealing; he's threatened by the same qualities that impressed the Bobs
jokes.explanation: TPS reports as Lumbergh's greatest grievance against Peter is a running gag callback that works. The irony — Lumbergh's most damning evidence is exactly what made the Bobs love Peter — deepens the satire about what's actually valued in corporate culture.

jokes.text: Bobs tell Lumbergh: 'The problem isn't with Peter. It's that you haven't challenged him enough to get him really motivated.'
jokes.setup: Lumbergh has tried to dismiss Peter; Bobs push back
jokes.punchline: The Bobs reframe Peter's total disengagement as Lumbergh's management failure — turning the critique around on the manager, leaving Lumbergh literally speechless
jokes.explanation: The Bobs are turning Lumbergh's own HR-speak language back on him — 'challenged enough,' 'really motivated' — the same empty vocabulary he would use on subordinates. Watching Lumbergh squirm under corporate-speak he's used to wielding is delightful. 'There it is,' says Slydell, with satisfaction.

jokes.text: Bob Slydell asks Lumbergh how much time he spends per week on TPS reports — Lumbergh cannot answer
jokes.setup: Lumbergh has cited TPS reports as evidence of Peter's failure; Slydell turns it around
jokes.punchline: Long, painful pause (17 seconds of silence/mumbling from Lumbergh) — Lumbergh, the TPS report enforcer, cannot quantify or justify the value of TPS reports when directly challenged
jokes.explanation: The long silence is the entire joke, and it's devastating. Lumbergh has tormented Peter about TPS reports for the entire film; now asked to justify them, he has nothing. The [41:07] timestamp gap before 'Yeah...' at [41:17] represents a full ten-second-plus beat of silence/mumbling that is purely comedic. It's the TPS report gag's perfect payoff: the bureaucratic arbiter cannot defend his own bureaucracy. This is the kind of joke that works better on screen than on the page — the silence IS the punchline.

jokes.text: Cut from Lumbergh's paralyzed non-answer directly to 'Damn, it feels good to be a gangsta' — Peter strutting out of the office to Geto Boys
jokes.setup: Lumbergh is frozen and humiliated mid-meeting; we've just seen the TPS regime crumble
jokes.punchline: Hard cut to Peter walking out of the building in slow motion to hardcore hip-hop — the most grandiose possible exit for a man who just confessed to doing 15 minutes of work per week
jokes.explanation: One of the great comic visual/music gags in 1990s film comedy. The juxtaposition of Peter's mundane rebellion (skipping work, being honest in an interview) with the hyper-masculine gangsta posturing of the Geto Boys track is perfectly calibrated absurdism. It makes Peter's small victories feel enormous — and the film is self-aware that this is comic hyperbole. The slow-motion walk earns its swagger because of everything we've just watched. Iconic.

jokes.text: Lawrence: 'Hey, Peter, man! Check out channel nine, it's the breast exams. Whoo!'
jokes.setup: Peter has arrived home after his triumphant exit, riding the high of the Geto Boys sequence
jokes.punchline: Lawrence's completely guileless greeting — cutting from Peter's cinematic triumph to his neighbor watching breast exam TV in the middle of the day — is the perfect deflating button on the sequence
jokes.explanation: Lawrence as comic foil/anchor to reality is perfect deployment. The Geto Boys sequence has made Peter feel like a gangsta — then we cut to his neighbor watching medical programming with juvenile enthusiasm. 'Channel nine' grounds the film back in suburban mediocrity after the cinematic swell. It's a perfect button: funny, character-specific to Lawrence, and deflating in the best way.

jokes.text: Geto Boys 'Damn It Feels Good to Be a Gangsta' plays over Peter casually greeting Dom in the hallway — the ultra-hard gangsta anthem underscores the mundane office exchange
jokes.setup: Hard-core Geto Boys rap about gangsta life, crime, and the streets
jokes.punchline: The scene it soundtracks is a completely mundane hallway greeting between two office workers
jokes.explanation: Mike Judge's signature move: the ironic contrast between the maximally aggressive soundtrack and the soul-crushing banality of office life. The gap between 'Damn it feels good to be a gangsta' and 'Hi, Peter / Oh, hi, Dom' is enormous and perfectly executed. The music itself becomes the joke's delivery mechanism — economy is near-perfect because no dialogue is needed. This is a 8+ moment because the juxtaposition is both original in this context and structurally airtight.

jokes.text: Bill Lumbergh's glacially slow, passive-aggressive TPS report check-in: 'So... Peter... what's happening? Ahh, now, are you going to go ahead... and have those T.P.S. reports for us this afternoon?'
jokes.setup: Bill appears with his signature coffee mug, preparing to deliver a mundane work request
jokes.punchline: His delivery is so drawn-out, so performatively casual, and so laden with corporate non-speak ('go ahead and') that the request itself becomes an act of psychological torture
jokes.explanation: Lumbergh is one of cinema's great comic creations. Every one of his lines is a masterpiece of passive-aggressive corporate speech — 'go ahead and,' the trailing ellipses in his delivery, the false casualness. Character integration is near-perfect: no one else in the film could deliver this. It has become a cultural touchstone for bad bosses. Scores 8+ because Lumbergh's character is so precisely crafted that every appearance is funny purely from who he is.

jokes.text: Peter flatly tells his boss 'No' to the TPS report request, then tells Lumbergh he's busy and to 'go ahead and come back another time' — mirroring Lumbergh's own verbal tics back at him
jokes.setup: Lumbergh asks Peter about the TPS reports in his usual domineering-but-casual way, expecting compliance
jokes.punchline: Peter says 'No' with zero affect, then uses Lumbergh's own corporate filler language ('go ahead and') to dismiss him
jokes.explanation: This is the film's first great cathartic payoff. Peter weaponizing Lumbergh's own speech patterns against him — 'I'm going to have to ask you to go ahead and come back another time' — is exceptionally crafted. It demonstrates character transformation, linguistic precision, and delivers a vicarious thrill for everyone who ever wanted to say no to a Bill Lumbergh. The flat delivery makes it funnier. This is a genuine 8.5 — it's close to the reference anchor quality, specific, quotable, and perfectly executed.

jokes.text: Bill's reaction to learning the Bobs called Peter at home: 'Uh, I wasn't aware of a meeting with them.' Then: 'That sounds good, Peter... we'll go ahead and get this all fixed up for you. Great.' — Lumbergh visibly deflated but masking it
jokes.setup: Lumbergh expects to be in total control; Peter invokes the Bobs as a trump card
jokes.punchline: Lumbergh is caught off-guard but immediately retreats into his hollow corporate affirmations, revealing that his power is entirely performative
jokes.explanation: The humor is in Lumbergh's barely-concealed impotence — his 'great' and 'that sounds good' are deflections of a man who has just been outmaneuvered. Funny because it reveals the hollowness behind his authority. Good character comedy, though it's secondary to joke #3.

jokes.text: Bill tells Milton mid-sentence about being moved to storage B, cutting off Milton's legitimate paycheck complaint without a beat
jokes.setup: Milton tries to raise a real problem (missing paycheck); Lumbergh has already stopped listening
jokes.punchline: Without acknowledging Milton's words, Bill announces he's being moved to 'storage B' — the ultimate corporate dismissal
jokes.explanation: The comedy of erasure — Milton's problems are so thoroughly ignored that Lumbergh doesn't even let him finish his sentence before announcing something worse. It's both Lumbergh character comedy and cringe, and it escalates Milton's slow-burn humiliation effectively.

jokes.text: Bob Porter: 'You've been missing a lot of work lately.' Peter: 'I wouldn't say I've been missing it, Bob.'
jokes.setup: Bob uses 'missing work' in the sense of absenteeism — a standard HR confrontation opener
jokes.punchline: Peter reinterprets 'missing' as 'missing emotionally' — a perfect, deadpan wordplay pivot that doubles as a thesis statement for the whole film
jokes.explanation: One of the greatest single-line jokes in the film and arguably one of the best wordplay lines in workplace comedy. It's simultaneously a clever pun, a character revelation, a philosophy statement, and it lands perfectly off the deadpan delivery. Economy is 10/10 — seven words that do the work of a monologue. The Bobs even validate it ('Good one. / Oh, that's terrific, Peter') which acts as an in-universe laugh track. This is comparable to the 8.0 anchor and arguably surpasses it in quotability and economy. Easily the standout line of this reel.

jokes.text: Bob Slydell: 'Oh, that's terrific, Peter' — the Bobs laugh appreciatively at Peter's joke about not missing work
jokes.setup: Peter has just made the 'missing it' joke
jokes.punchline: The efficiency consultants — hired to fire people — are charmed and amused by the very slacker they should be targeting, validating Peter's new attitude as actually winning
jokes.explanation: The Bobs' delighted reaction amplifies joke #7 and sets up the absurd logic of Peter's promotion. Their enthusiasm for someone who openly doesn't care about work is good irony — the consultants mistake authentic detachment for confident leadership. Functional comedic beat that serves the narrative.

jokes.text: Bob Porter struggles to pronounce 'Nagheenanajar,' trails off into 'Naga... gonna work here anymore, anyway' — accidentally naming the layoff policy
jokes.setup: Porter starts to announce Samir's surname and can't pronounce it
jokes.punchline: He stumbles into 'Naga-gonna work here anymore' — a malapropism that doubles as a corporate euphemism for firing someone
jokes.explanation: A clever bit of wordplay that emerges naturally from the character's incompetence. The stumbling pronunciation becoming an accidental HR announcement is both funny and darkly satirical — these consultants are firing people they can't even name. Well-crafted, memorable, and character-specific.

jokes.text: Slydell explains they fire people on Fridays because studies show there's 'less chance of an incident' — delivered with absolute sincerity
jokes.setup: Peter asks if Samir and Michael know they're being fired
jokes.punchline: Slydell matter-of-factly explains the Friday firing strategy as if it's responsible HR practice, the implicit 'incident' being violence or breakdown
jokes.explanation: Dark corporate humor executed with precision. The 'incident' euphemism is loaded — it implies rage-quitting or worse — and Slydell's clinical delivery makes it funnier. Genuine dark comedy that also says something true about corporate culture.

jokes.text: The Bobs offer Peter a promotion — 'as many as four people working right underneath you' — right after announcing his friends will be fired, and Peter reacts with 'Wow!'
jokes.setup: Peter has just heard his two best friends are being laid off
jokes.punchline: He's simultaneously being offered a promotion. His 'Wow!' reads as either darkly comic self-interest or shock — the audience doesn't know which yet
jokes.explanation: The situational irony is strong — the cruelty of corporate logic laid bare. Peter's 'Wow' is ambiguous in a productive way. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Michael is heard off-screen coaxing his computer: 'That's it. That's exactly what I need. Give it to me. Come on, you little fucker, let's go... Let's do that. Let's do exactly that, you little fuck—' then is suddenly cut off
jokes.setup: Serious conversation about Samir and Michael's layoffs in the meeting room
jokes.punchline: Michael is obliviously having an increasingly intimate argument/negotiation with his computer, completely unaware of the stakes being discussed nearby
jokes.explanation: Perfect character comedy — Michael's violent, almost erotic relationship with his computer is entirely consistent with who he is. The irony that he's cursing out a computer while his job is being terminated in the next room is funny and reveals character. The abrupt cutoff adds to the effect.

jokes.text: Michael to Peter: 'I know you had this religious experience or whatever... but get your shit together, or you're gonna get canned.'
jokes.setup: Peter is trying to give Michael a serious life pep talk about their future
jokes.punchline: Michael dismisses Peter's enlightenment as 'religious experience or whatever' and pivots to telling the person who just got promoted that HE needs to get his act together
jokes.explanation: Good irony — Michael is advising Peter to keep his job right before Peter reveals he's being promoted while Michael is fired. The dramatic irony elevates an otherwise average line.

jokes.text: 'This sounds familiar.' / 'They did it in Superman III.' / Peter: 'Right, uh—' / Michael: 'An underrated movie, actually.'
jokes.setup: Michael describes the decimal-skimming scheme as if it's a novel idea
jokes.punchline: Samir immediately calls out the Superman III reference; Michael's defensive 'underrated movie, actually' is both a deflection and a perfectly absurd non-sequitur in this context
jokes.explanation: One of the best small jokes in this reel. 'An underrated movie, actually' is a perfectly economical deflection — Michael is so committed to his genius that he defends the film he plagiarized rather than the scheme. The self-awareness of the Superman III reference (the film is literally doing the same scheme) adds a meta layer. Genuinely funny and very quotable.

jokes.text: Michael refuses: 'It's not worth the risk. I got a good job.' — delivered with complete sincerity right before Peter says 'What if you didn't have a good job?'
jokes.setup: Michael says he won't do the scheme because he has a good job to protect
jokes.punchline: Peter immediately counters with 'What if you didn't have a good job?' — revealing that Michael's objection is about to become moot
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony is fully loaded here — we know Michael is being fired; Michael doesn't. Peter's 'What if you didn't have a good job?' lands as both a genuinely cruel tease for the audience and a structurally perfect setup-punchline. The economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Samir and I are the best programmers they got. You haven't been showing up, and you get to keep your job. Actually, I'm being promoted.'
jokes.setup: Michael asserts his job security based on competence
jokes.punchline: Peter confirms he's being promoted — the worst possible outcome for Michael's logic
jokes.explanation: The 'actually, I'm being promoted' beat is a great punctuation on Michael's argument. The setup is Michael laying out exactly why the system makes no sense, and Peter confirming the system makes no sense. Well-structured, funny exchange.

jokes.text: Peter's speech: 'Human beings were not meant to sit in little cubicles, staring at computer screens all day, filling out useless forms, and listening to eight different bosses drone on about mission statements.'
jokes.setup: Peter is delivering an earnest speech about the meaninglessness of corporate existence
jokes.punchline: The specificity of 'eight different bosses' and 'mission statements' tips the speech from sincere into absurd self-awareness — it's both a genuine lament and a comedic inventory
jokes.explanation: One of the film's thesis-statement speeches. Funny because it's true and because the specificity ('eight different bosses') is so perfectly calibrated. It resonates with office workers everywhere. Not the biggest laugh but high quotability and cultural resonance.

jokes.text: Michael, after Peter's heartfelt speech about human dignity: 'I told those fudgepackers I liked Michael Bolton's music.' Peter: 'Ohh. That is not right, Michael.'
jokes.setup: Peter has just delivered an earnest speech about meaningful existence and wasted years
jokes.punchline: Michael's most pressing response is about being forced to admit he likes the singer Michael Bolton — a catastrophic collision of registers
jokes.explanation: A callback to Michael's ongoing humiliation about sharing a name with the soft-rock singer. The genius is in the tonal collision — Peter is talking about the meaning of life and Michael's contribution is that he was forced to admit to liking Michael Bolton. Peter's 'That is not right, Michael' is the perfect deadpan straight-man response. High character integration: only this specific Michael could deliver this line. 8+ justified.

jokes.text: Peter to Samir: 'This isn't Riyadh. They're not going to saw your hands off here. The worst they'd do is put you in a white-collar, minimum-security resort.'
jokes.setup: Samir refuses on the grounds that it's illegal
jokes.punchline: Peter's response compares American white-collar prosecution favorably to Saudi Arabian corporal punishment — the logic is both absurd and strangely coherent
jokes.explanation: Mike Judge's dark comedy instincts at work — Peter's argument is genuinely persuasive by the worst possible standards. The Riyadh reference is specific and unexpected. Good joke with real edge.

jokes.text: Peter: 'They have conjugal visits there.' / Michael: 'Shit, we should be so lucky. They have conjugal visits. I'm a free man. I haven't had a conjugal visit in six months.'
jokes.setup: Peter is pitching prison as not that bad
jokes.punchline: Michael reveals prison's conjugal visits sound better than his current sex life — he hasn't had sex in six months as a free man
jokes.explanation: Michael's pathetic love life being revealed as worse than federal prison is a great character moment. The specificity of 'six months' adds to the pathos-comedy blend. Very character-specific — only Michael would interpret this as a point in the scheme's favor.

jokes.text: Samir's only remaining question before agreeing to commit federal fraud: 'In this conjugal visits, you can have sex with women?' / Peter: 'Yep, you sure can.' / Samir: 'OK, I'll do it.'
jokes.setup: The whole pitch has been about justice, dignity, and opportunity; Samir has one dealbreaker question
jokes.punchline: His entire moral calculus hinges entirely on heterosexual prison sex — and once confirmed, he immediately commits to federal crime
jokes.explanation: A perfectly structured comedic escalation. The whole pitch culminating in Samir's singular concern — are the conjugal visits with women — and that being the deciding factor is both a great character revelation and a structurally perfect joke. Peter's 'Yep, you sure can' and Samir's instant 'OK, I'll do it' is impeccably timed. This is 8+ territory: specific, character-integrated, well-structured, and delivers a genuine eruption laugh.

jokes.text: Peter: 'That's what I'm talking about when I talk about America!'
jokes.setup: Samir has just agreed to commit federal embezzlement because prison allegedly has women for conjugal visits
jokes.punchline: Peter frames this as a patriotic moment — the American Dream, as defined by Peter, is heterosexual prison sex as a criminal incentive
jokes.explanation: Peter's celebration of Samir's decision as an American values moment is a great satirical button on the scene. The irony is rich — the immigrant is persuaded to commit fraud by a promise of prison sex, and this is framed as the land of opportunity. Very well-timed.

jokes.text: They swear to God and Allah that nobody will know — immediately followed by Lawrence's voice from next door: 'Don't worry, man! I won't tell anyone, either.'
jokes.setup: The three conspirators solemnly swear secrecy — no family, no girlfriends, nobody
jokes.punchline: Lawrence, Peter's neighbor, has been listening through the wall the whole time and cheerfully volunteers himself into the secret
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom-adjacent setup-punchline with excellent structure. The solemnity of the oath is immediately punctured by Lawrence's oblivious participation. Peter's 'What the fuck is that? / Don't worry. He's cool.' caps it perfectly. Good construction.

jokes.text: Ice Cube's 'It Was a Good Day' plays over a montage of the scheme being executed successfully
jokes.setup: The three are committing federal embezzlement
jokes.punchline: Ice Cube's famous feel-good anthem ('I didn't even have to use my AK / Today was a good day') celebrates the crime with the most triumphant possible music
jokes.explanation: Mike Judge's use of hip-hop throughout the film is a consistent comedy engine. Using 'It Was a Good Day' for the crime montage is structurally the same joke as the opening Geto Boys but specifically resonant — it's literally 'today was a good day' as a celebration of federal fraud by three office workers. Well-executed.

jokes.text: Michael and Peter after apparently having done something — 'That was easy.' / 'Yeah, I guess it was.' / 'What'd you do with the—' — immediately interrupted by Drew before they can finish the sentence
jokes.setup: We cut from Ice Cube's 'It Was a Good Day' (the most perfect musical irony) to the guys after completing the scheme
jokes.punchline: The whole heist is summarized in 'That was easy' — the film completely skips the caper and delivers the aftermath with maximum casualness
jokes.explanation: The ellipsis joke — skipping the heist entirely and just saying 'that was easy' — is a confident structural choice that's also funny. The interrupted sentence adds to the joke.

jokes.text: Tom Smykowski, caught attempting suicide in the garage, tries to cover: 'I was having some trouble with the shifter here. It's jammed. I—I couldn't get it into drive. I—I—I mean, reverse.'
jokes.setup: Tom's wife catches him running the car in a closed garage in an apparent suicide attempt
jokes.punchline: His cover story is that the shifter was jammed — and his slip from 'drive' to 'reverse' perfectly reveals he hadn't thought this lie through at all
jokes.explanation: The 'drive/reverse' slip is a beautiful small detail — Tom's lie is so hastily constructed that he can't even keep his car directions straight. It's cringe comedy with a surprisingly precise verbal gag embedded in it. The specific nature of the error elevates this beyond generic awkward-lie comedy.

jokes.text: Drew: 'As soon as he backs out of his driveway... Bam! He gets slammed big-time by a drunk driver. Broke both his wrists, legs, a couple of ribs, his back — but he's getting a huge settlement out of this. Like seven figures. He's throwing a big party this weekend to celebrate.'
jokes.setup: Tom survived his suicide attempt and decides to live
jokes.punchline: He immediately gets catastrophically injured by a drunk driver — but the punchline is that the settlement makes him a millionaire, so this series of disasters ends in triumph, and he's throwing a party
jokes.explanation: One of the film's great dark comedy setpieces. The escalation is structurally perfect: attempted suicide → decides to live → immediately nearly killed by drunk driver → BUT seven figures → celebration party. Each beat subverts the previous one. The pivot from catastrophe to celebration is a genuinely well-constructed dark joke with real emotional whiplash. 8+ justified by the structural elegance of the reversal-within-reversal.

jokes.text: Drew, describing Tom's party: 'I'm thinking I might take that new chick from logistics. Things go well, I might be showing her my "Oh" face. Oh, oh, oh... You know what I'm talking about. Oh.'
jokes.setup: Drew casually transitions from Tom's near-death/miracle story to his own plans for getting laid at the subsequent party
jokes.punchline: The 'Oh face' bit — Drew demonstrating his own orgasm face in a workplace context — is both a character moment and an extended cringe gag
jokes.explanation: The 'Oh face' has become one of the film's most quoted lines. Drew's transition from discussing a near-fatal accident/miracle to planning his seduction strategy reveals a gloriously self-absorbed character. High quotability; becomes a callback later in this same reel.

jokes.text: Drew: 'Sort of. Broke both his wrists, legs, a couple of ribs, his back — but he's getting a huge settlement out of this. Like seven figures. He's throwing a big party this weekend to celebrate. We're all invited.'
jokes.setup: 'Is he OK?' / 'Sort of.'
jokes.punchline: The list of catastrophic injuries transitions directly into 'huge settlement... big party... we're all invited' as if this is a normal event
jokes.explanation: The pivot from medical catastrophe to party invitation is well-executed. 'Sort of' is a great single-word setup. The whole Tom story is a contained comedic narrative with good structure.

jokes.text: Samir: 'I can't believe they had security escort us out. It's not like we're going to steal something.' — a beat — Peter: 'I stole something.' / Michael: 'Oh, yeah. I guess we all did.'
jokes.setup: Samir is indignant about being escorted out by security as if they were criminals
jokes.punchline: Peter admits he stole something — and they all realize they literally just committed federal fraud and are definitely criminals
jokes.explanation: Perfectly constructed irony — Samir's righteous indignation about being treated like a thief while literally being a thief. The escalating admissions ('I stole something.' / 'Oh, yeah. I guess we all did.') work beautifully. Great structure and economy.

jokes.text: Peter: 'Call it a going-away present.' — visual reveal of Peter having stolen the giant printer/copier machine that the guys have been trying to destroy
jokes.setup: Peter mentions he stole something; Michael and Samir ask what
jokes.punchline: He stole the printer — the object of the film's most cathartic destruction fantasy, now sitting in his apartment
jokes.explanation: The printer is an established symbol of workplace misery throughout the film. Peter stealing it as a 'going-away present' is a great visual callback that pays off a running gag and reveals character (he's not done with this printer). 8+ justified by the callback payoff quality and the visual impact of seeing the printer in his apartment.

jokes.text: Peter, being unable to tell Joanna what they were celebrating: 'Oh, um... I'm not really at liberty to talk about it. I really can't.'
jokes.setup: Joanna asks what they were celebrating
jokes.punchline: Peter's formal 'I'm not at liberty to discuss it' — legal secrecy language for a crime he just committed — is both pompous and self-incriminating in a funny way
jokes.explanation: Decent beat — the pomposity of the secrecy language is funny but not exceptional. It's a transitional joke that sets up the bigger confession scene.

jokes.text: Peter explains the embezzlement scheme in full detail to Joanna despite having just sworn an oath of secrecy thirty seconds of screen time earlier
jokes.setup: Peter solemnly swore 'no family members, no girlfriends' would know about the scheme
jokes.punchline: He immediately tells his girlfriend the entire scheme in complete technical detail — the oath lasted approximately one date
jokes.explanation: The callback to the oath is implicit but clear to attentive viewers. Peter's total inability to maintain secrecy despite his elaborate oath is good character comedy, though the joke lives more in the structural irony than in a single great line.

jokes.text: Peter's increasingly desperate explanation: 'It's aggregate, so I'm talking about fractions of a penny... and uh, over time, they add up to a lot.' Joanna: 'Oh OK. So you're gonna make a lot of money, right?' Peter: 'Yeah.' 'Right. It's not yours?'
jokes.setup: Peter uses technical jargon to try to obscure the basic moral reality of what he's doing
jokes.punchline: Joanna cuts straight through the obfuscation with: 'It's not yours?' — the simplest possible moral question that destroys his entire rhetorical structure
jokes.explanation: Joanna functions as a perfectly calibrated straight-man here. Peter's technical obfuscation is funny; Joanna cutting through it with 'It's not yours?' is funnier. The structure is excellent — the more elaborate Peter's justification, the more devastating the simple question. This scene is a small masterpiece of comedic deflation.

jokes.text: Peter's 7-Eleven penny-tray analogy for why the theft is acceptable, escalating to: 'But we do it from a much bigger tray and we do it a couple of million times.'
jokes.setup: Peter tries to minimize the scale of the crime by comparing it to taking a penny from the communal tray
jokes.punchline: His own analogy collapses when he admits the scale: millions of times, from a much bigger tray — his own logic refutes his argument
jokes.explanation: The 7-Eleven tray analogy is a great piece of motivated reasoning comedy — Peter is so committed to the logic that he walks himself right into the admission that defeats his own argument. Good structure, earned laugh.

jokes.text: Peter: 'You'd take a penny from the tray.' / Joanna: 'From the crippled children?' / Peter: 'No, that's the jar. I'm talking about the tray — the pennies for everybody.'
jokes.setup: Peter uses the communal penny tray as a moral comparison
jokes.punchline: Joanna assumes he means the charity jar for crippled children — an escalation that makes Peter's justification even more damning before he clarifies
jokes.explanation: A quick, well-structured misdirection. Joanna's escalation to 'from the crippled children?' is both funny in itself and strategically brilliant — it makes Peter seem even worse for a moment before the clarification. Good economy and structure.

jokes.text: Peter: 'The Nazis had pieces of flair that they made the Jews wear.'
jokes.setup: Peter is trying to justify the theft by saying Chotchkie's (Joanna's workplace) is also wrong for making her wear 'flair'
jokes.punchline: His argument that mandatory flair is equivalent to Nazi persecution of Jews is so wildly disproportionate that it short-circuits the conversation entirely
jokes.explanation: One of the film's most quotable lines. Peter's absurd rhetorical escalation — equating restaurant flair requirements to the Holocaust — is simultaneously outrageous, funny, and reveals the depth of his moral sophistry. It's a reductio ad Hitlerum deployed sincerely by a man trying to justify his crimes, which makes it both funnier and more character-revealing. The economy is exceptional — one sentence that destroys his entire argument by overplaying it. High quotability score justified.

jokes.text: Tom Smykowski, in a full-body cast at a barbecue, apologizes for 'not getting up' — delivered with a laugh
jokes.setup: Peter introduces Joanna to Tom at the barbecue; Tom is in a full-body cast from his car accident
jokes.punchline: 'Forgive me for not getting up' — the most understated possible acknowledgment of his catastrophic physical state
jokes.explanation: Classic dark deadpan — a man who survived a suicide attempt and a drunk driving accident hosting a party in a full-body cast, apologizing for not getting up. The gap between the horror of the situation and the social politeness of the line is funny. Well-executed, if familiar as a type.

jokes.text: Tom shows Peter his prototype invention — Peter's reaction: 'Huh... that's... that's exactly as you described it.'
jokes.setup: Tom excitedly presents what he implies is a great invention
jokes.punchline: Peter's 'that's exactly as you described it' — clearly masking that the thing is exactly as bad as described — is a masterpiece of diplomatic understatement
jokes.explanation: One of the film's quieter gems. Peter's response — 'that's exactly as you described it' — perfectly conveys that he is saying nothing positive while technically saying nothing negative. The fact that we never see the invention makes it funnier, as the audience imagines something terrible. Great economy and implied visual comedy.

jokes.text: Tom's life advice to Peter: 'Maybe I didn't whine as much... But I bet I hated my job even more than you, and I'd been doing it for over thirty years.' Then: 'Just remember, if you hang in there long enough, good things can happen in this world. I mean, look at me.'
jokes.setup: Tom is dispensing wisdom about persevering through job unhappiness
jokes.punchline: His example of 'good things happening if you hang in there' is himself: a man who had to survive a suicide attempt AND a drunk driving accident AND break most of his bones to get a lottery-ticket settlement — this is the film's definition of success
jokes.explanation: 'Look at me' — delivered in a full-body cast after a suicide attempt and drunk driving accident — is a brilliantly dark punchline. Tom has completely internalized this disaster as a success story, and his advice is sincere. The film uses this to comment on how people survive terrible jobs: they endure until something calamitous happens to free them. Well-structured dark comedy.

jokes.text: Rob the lawyer: 'Conjugal visits? Not that I know of. Minimum-security prison is no picnic... The trick is kick someone's ass the first day, or become someone's bitch.'
jokes.setup: Michael and Samir are nervously asking about prison conjugal visits — the entire basis for Samir agreeing to commit fraud
jokes.punchline: The lawyer who actually knows about prison delivers the reality check: no conjugal visits, and survival requires either violence or sexual submission
jokes.explanation: A devastating callback payoff — the entire scheme was predicated on conjugal visits being available, and the first real expert they encounter immediately debunks this. Rob's casual delivery of prison survival strategy ('kick someone's ass or become someone's bitch') is funny and also retroactively recontextualizes Samir's decision. The unspoken reaction of Michael and Samir makes this funnier.

jokes.text: Drew, on seeing Peter is with Joanna from Chotchkie's: 'Make sure you wear a rubber, dude.'
jokes.setup: Drew casually congratulates Peter on being with Joanna
jokes.punchline: The unsolicited safe-sex advice is Drew's way of signaling he knows something about Joanna's history — the punchline is delivered before the payload is explained
jokes.explanation: Classic setup for the Lumbergh revelation. The rubber joke is functional but its main value is as a setup. The structure — advice first, explanation second — is good.

jokes.text: Drew: 'She gets around. All right? She does, does she? Oh, yeah. Like a record.' Then: 'Hell, Lumbergh fucked her.'
jokes.setup: Peter asks who Joanna has been with
jokes.punchline: The name 'Lumbergh' — delivered casually as the first example — lands as the worst possible revelation, the equivalent of learning your girlfriend slept with Satan
jokes.explanation: One of the film's great jokes and a genuine 8+ moment. The delivery is everything: Drew is so casual ('Hell, Lumbergh fucked her'), as if Lumbergh is just another name on a list, but to Peter (and the audience) it's the worst possible answer. The structure is perfect — building through 'like a record' and then dropping Lumbergh as if it's an afterthought. Peter's cut-to reaction ('Lumbergh?') with the full pause before is exactly right. This rivals the reference anchors for structural perfection.

jokes.text: Peter's silent, shell-shocked reaction beat — the cut to him sitting alone, processing 'Lumbergh?'
jokes.setup: Drew has just revealed Lumbergh slept with Joanna
jokes.punchline: Peter's stunned silence — 'Lumbergh?' — is the comedic processing of an almost cosmically unfair piece of information
jokes.explanation: The reaction beat is as funny as the revelation itself — Peter's single-word 'Lumbergh?' with the pause is a perfect comedic beat. The audience laughs at his horror. Well-staged and well-performed.

jokes.text: Drew: 'Hell, Lumbergh fucked her.'
jokes.setup: Drew is listing examples of Joanna's romantic history to prove his point
jokes.punchline: The name drop: Bill Lumbergh — Peter's boss, the person who represents everything Peter despises — is revealed to have a history with Joanna
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the film and certainly the best setup for a running gag in this reel. The comedic payload is enormous: Lumbergh has been established as Peter's nemesis, the embodiment of everything soul-crushing and degrading about corporate life, and Drew drops this information with casual matter-of-factness ('Hell, Lumbergh fucked her') as if it's a minor biographical detail. The specificity of 'Hell' as an intensifier — not 'even' or 'like' — is perfect Drew. The delivery in context is devastating. Five words, maximum damage. It earns its high scores because of the character integration (only Lumbergh could produce this reaction), the economy, and the explosive impact on the narrative.

jokes.text: Peter's inner monologue/nightmare: imagining Lumbergh's face saying 'If you could just move a little bit to the left... That's it. Great. Peter, what's happening? Um, could you give me those T.P.S. reports ASAP, OK?'
jokes.setup: Peter is horrified by the revelation that Lumbergh slept with Joanna
jokes.punchline: His mind conjures Lumbergh's sex life as an extension of his office behavior — Lumbergh giving Joanna work instructions during sex, using his exact office speech patterns ('If you could just move a little to the left... That's it. Great.')
jokes.explanation: The single funniest moment in this reel and one of the best jokes in the film. Taking Lumbergh's signature passive-aggressive office-speak — 'if you could just move a little bit to the left... That's it. Great.' and 'Peter, what's happening? Could you give me those T.P.S. reports ASAP?' — and transplanting it verbatim into a sexual context is a stroke of comedic genius. It requires the entire film's worth of Lumbergh characterization to land, it's perfectly character-integrated, deeply original, and the execution is flawless. This is comfortably in the 9+ tier — comparable to the 'Snip, snap!' anchor in its use of a character's established verbal tic being applied to a devastating new context. The 'Oh!' reaction that closes it is the perfect button.

jokes.text: Peter confronts Joanna about Lumbergh mid-argument about the scheme: 'Maybe it wasn't such a good idea for you to sleep with Lumbergh.' / Joanna: 'Oh, right, Lumbergh. Aah! Oh...God...Lumbergh!'
jokes.setup: Joanna is questioning the ethics of the scheme; Peter pivots to the Lumbergh revelation
jokes.punchline: Joanna's involuntary shudder at the name — 'Oh... God... Lumbergh!' — suggests even she is horrified by the memory, which somehow makes Peter feel worse
jokes.explanation: Joanna's visceral 'Oh...God...Lumbergh!' reaction is funny and also darkly suggests that even she regrets it — which doesn't comfort Peter at all. Good character comedy with a satisfying callback.

jokes.text: Joanna: 'Oh, he's not that disgusting.' — immediately after Peter calls Lumbergh 'my unholy, disgusting pig of a boss'
jokes.setup: Peter is catastrophizing about Lumbergh
jokes.punchline: Joanna's mild defense of Lumbergh — 'he's not that disgusting' — is a horrifying non-apology that makes everything worse
jokes.explanation: Joanna's calibrated defense — not 'he's a good person,' just 'not that disgusting' — is a great small joke. It's precisely calibrated to be the most damning possible partial defense.

jokes.text: Joanna: 'What are you? You think you're an angel? No, you're just this penny-stealing wannabe criminal man.'
jokes.setup: Peter is judging Joanna for her past with Lumbergh
jokes.punchline: Joanna correctly identifies Peter as a criminal — 'penny-stealing wannabe criminal man' — which both deflates his moral high ground and is objectively accurate
jokes.explanation: 'Penny-stealing wannabe criminal man' is a great insult because it's both accurate and deflating — Joanna cuts Peter's moral indignation off at the knees by reminding him he literally just admitted to federal fraud. The callback structure is tight.

jokes.text: Peter: 'Yeah, well, that may be. But at least I never slept with Lumbergh.'
jokes.setup: Joanna has just correctly identified Peter as a criminal
jokes.punchline: Peter's rejoinder is not to deny being a criminal — he concedes the point — but doubles down on the Lumbergh issue as his moral trump card
jokes.explanation: 'Yeah, well, that may be. But at least I never slept with Lumbergh.' — the concession of his criminality to maintain his Lumbergh objection is a great character beat. Peter's hierarchy of sins (Lumbergh > federal fraud) is both absurd and character-consistent.

jokes.text: Joanna's exit line: 'Call me when you grow up. Wait — that's probably never gonna happen. So don't call me, OK?' followed by Peter's: 'Say hello to Lumbergh for me!'
jokes.setup: Joanna is making a dramatic exit from Peter's car
jokes.punchline: Peter's parting shot — 'Say hello to Lumbergh for me!' — is both petty and funny; a man so consumed by Lumbergh that it's his closing statement in a breakup
jokes.explanation: 'Say hello to Lumbergh for me' as a breakup parting shot is good — it shows Peter is so consumed by Lumbergh that the man has invaded even his personal relationships. Good button on the scene.

jokes.text: Drew, to Peter after the breakup: 'Hell, Lumbergh fucked her. Lumbergh fucked her. That is great. I mean, she was seeing the "Oh" face for sure. Ohh, ohh, ohh.'
jokes.setup: Peter has just broken up with his girlfriend over the Lumbergh revelation
jokes.punchline: Drew is completely delighted by this, repeating 'Lumbergh fucked her' with glee and invoking his own 'Oh face' bit in the context of Lumbergh, adding a new layer of horror to both
jokes.explanation: A double callback — Drew's 'Oh face' now applied to Lumbergh. The mental image of Lumbergh's 'Oh face' is an inspired bit of implied horror comedy. Drew's gleeful insensitivity about Peter's breakup is also very consistent with his character.

jokes.text: Joanna's boss Stan notices she's wearing only 15 pieces of flair — 'Your lack of flair, because, uh, I'm counting, and I only see fifteen pieces.'
jokes.setup: We cut from Peter's nightmare to Joanna at Chotchkie's being called in by her manager
jokes.punchline: Stan is auditing her flair with a count — 'fifteen pieces' — the bureaucratic precision of counting pieces of decorative flair as a performance metric is the joke
jokes.explanation: The flair audit is good cringe comedy — it's a system so petty and absurd that having a manager enforce it with literal counting is both funny and infuriating on the employee's behalf. The specific number 'fifteen' versus the minimum requirement sets up the standoff well. This scene builds to Joanna's breakout moment.

jokes.text: Joanna stands up, flips the bird (implied by 'There's my flair. OK? And this is me expressing myself.'), and quits: 'I hate this job. I hate this goddamn job, and I don't need it.'
jokes.setup: Stan has pushed Joanna to the breaking point; she decides to demonstrate actual self-expression
jokes.punchline: She flips the double bird as 'flair' — the ultimate inversion of the system — then quits, completing her arc as the film's other character who achieves freedom
jokes.explanation: One of the great cathartic comedy moments in the film. The middle finger(s) as 'flair' is the perfect ironic conclusion to the flair argument — she's providing maximum self-expression, just not the type Stan wanted. 'I hate this job. I hate this goddamn job, and I don't need it' is the audience's fantasy declaration. High impact because it's both funny and genuinely satisfying — the audience has been waiting for this. The parallel with Peter's earlier liberation gives it structural resonance.

jokes.text: The three discover $305,326.13 has been stolen in one night instead of small fractions over years — cascade of 'Shit. / Shit. / Son of a bitch. / Shit. / This is a fuck. / Shit.' — Samir's 'This is a fuck' as his English idiom breaks down under stress
jokes.setup: They check the account expecting a few dollars; find $305,326.13 has been extracted overnight
jokes.punchline: The cascade of profanity culminates in Samir's 'This is a fuck' — his idiom collapsing under the pressure, reducing a catastrophic revelation to broken English
jokes.explanation: The escalating profanity sequence is well-constructed dark comedy, but Samir's 'This is a fuck' is the specific gem — his English idioms have never quite worked throughout the film, and under maximum stress his brain produces 'This is a fuck' instead of 'This is fucked.' It's perfectly character-specific and unexpectedly poetic. 8+ for the specific Samir joke, which elevates the whole sequence.

jokes.text: Michael: 'I must have put a decimal point in the wrong place or something. I always do that. I always mess up some mundane detail.' / Peter: 'Oh! Well, this is not a mundane detail, Michael!'
jokes.setup: They are trying to understand how $305,000 was stolen overnight instead of fractions of a cent over years
jokes.punchline: Michael's self-assessment that he 'always messes up some mundane detail' applied to a 300k federal crime is a grotesque understatement; Peter's 'this is not a mundane detail' is the perfect straight-man response
jokes.explanation: Michael casually referring to embezzling $305,000 as a 'mundane detail' he messed up — and doing so with the resigned self-awareness of someone who always does this — is excellent character comedy. It's so specifically Michael: catastrophically incompetent but completely self-aware about it in the most useless way. 8+ justified by character specificity and the perfection of 'mundane detail.'

jokes.text: Michael: 'Quit getting pissed at me. This was all your idea, asshole.' — delivered in the middle of a crisis
jokes.setup: Peter is blaming Michael for the decimal error
jokes.punchline: Michael correctly points out that the entire scheme was Peter's idea — a fair point that lands as funny because it's both true and completely beside the point in this moment
jokes.explanation: Michael's anger is funny and fair, but it's a standard argument beat rather than an exceptional joke. Functional character comedy.

jokes.text: Cut from crisis meeting to the entire office singing 'Happy Birthday, Mr. Lumbergh' — a full office rendition, festive and oblivious
jokes.setup: The three are in a panic about $305,000 in stolen money and facing federal prison
jokes.punchline: Cut to: the whole office joyfully singing happy birthday to Bill Lumbergh — a man we have seen only as a villain — with full ceremony, as if he is beloved
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition cut — from federal crime panic to celebratory birthday party for Lumbergh — is structurally excellent. It reframes both scenes: the panic feels more absurd against the birthday's normalcy; Lumbergh's birthday party seems sinister given what we know. 'Happy Birthday, Mr. Lumbergh' (echoing 'Happy Birthday, Mr. President') adds an inadvertent grandeur to the horror.

jokes.text: Office workers singing 'Happy Birthday to You' and 'Happy Birthday, Mr. Lumbergh' cuts into the panic scene
jokes.setup: Peter, Michael, and Samir are in full crisis mode trying to figure out how to escape before Initech discovers the theft
jokes.punchline: The scene cuts to the entire office singing happy birthday to Lumbergh — the man they're trying to steal from, being celebrated by the people they're about to ruin
jokes.explanation: Good ironic juxtaposition. The cut from the trio's crisis to Lumbergh's birthday celebration is a classic comedic edit — the two scenes comment on each other. Lumbergh's pained smile and 'That is terrific' response to his own birthday party is also good character comedy — he seems to find even his own celebration vaguely unsatisfactory.

jokes.text: Bill Lumbergh receiving birthday cake: 'Looks terrific. Mmm... Oh, that is terrific. Just terrific. Thanks, everybody. I really, really appreciate it. It's very special.'
jokes.setup: Lumbergh is at his birthday party, receiving a cake from his employees
jokes.punchline: He delivers thanks in his exact signature speech pattern — 'terrific... just terrific... really, really appreciate it... very special' — the same hollow corporate positivity he uses to dismiss and demean employees, now applied to his own birthday
jokes.explanation: Lumbergh can't turn off the performance even at his own party. His 'terrific, just terrific' is the same phrase he uses to dismiss employees' problems. Character integration is near-perfect — this is utterly specific to Lumbergh and reveals the depth of his inauthenticity. After the Lumbergh sex fantasy, we're now primed to find everything he says funny.

jokes.text: Milton is told 'Now, Milton, don't be greedy. Let's pass it along and make sure everyone gets a piece.' Milton: 'But last time I didn't receive a piece and I was told—' Nina: 'Just pass.' ... Milton: 'The cake... There's lots of cake? The ratio of people to cake is too big.'
jokes.setup: Milton is being told to pass the birthday cake along before he takes any
jokes.punchline: Milton's escalating protest — first appealing to past injustice, then being cut off, then delivering the tragically logical observation 'The ratio of people to cake is too big' — is a perfect final Milton beat
jokes.explanation: 'The ratio of people to cake is too big' is a perfect Milton line — a brilliant, logical observation delivered with the flat specificity of someone who has been noting injustices with actuarial precision for years. It's both funny on its face and a character reveal: Milton does not get emotional, he catalogs. This caps the film's running Milton gag with a great line. 8+ is justified: the character integration is near-perfect, the line itself is quotable and original, and it closes a running thread with precision.

jokes.text: [Mumbles] I could set the building on fire.
jokes.setup: Milton is being pushed around by Bill Lumbergh and ignored, delivering his grievances in his trademark mumble
jokes.punchline: His quiet, muttered threat to commit arson — delivered with zero affect — is both a callback to his simmering resentment and a preview of the film's climax
jokes.explanation: This line earns its high score because it's maximally character-integrated — only Milton says this, only in this exact mumbled way — and because the audience already knows Milton is capable of it. The rewatch bonus is enormous: we know the building actually burns down. Deadpan delivery of a genuinely menacing threat is classic Mike Judge. Close to the 8-anchor quality.

jokes.text: Maybe we could launder the money. That's a great idea. OK, how do we do that? I don't know. I don't even know what it means. I was hoping you knew.
jokes.setup: The trio is in crisis trying to figure out how to cover up their embezzlement scheme
jokes.punchline: Michael enthusiastically endorses 'money laundering' as the solution but immediately admits he doesn't know what it means and was hoping someone else did
jokes.explanation: The two-beat structure is well-executed: the confident suggestion followed immediately by the deflation of total ignorance. The comedic escalation of 'great idea' → 'I don't know' → 'I don't even know what it means' is tight and well-paced. Character-integrated in that these are supposedly smart engineers who are completely hapless criminals.

jokes.text: I think coke dealers do it. OK, all right. Do we know any coke dealers?
jokes.setup: They're trying to figure out how money laundering works
jokes.punchline: The pivot from vague criminal theory to earnestly asking if they have any drug dealer contacts lands on the haplessness of these would-be criminals
jokes.explanation: Solid functional comedy. The absurd reasonableness of the question ('Do we know any coke dealers?') works because of the deadpan sincerity. Good economy, sets up the magazine salesman joke to come.

jokes.text: My cousin's a cokehead.
jokes.setup: Peter asks if they know any coke dealers
jokes.punchline: Samir's earnest, slightly-off answer — a cokehead is not a coke dealer — delivered with complete sincerity, landing on the gap between what was asked and what was offered
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum comedy. The beat that follows (the pause before 'Fuck') elevates it further. Samir's total sincerity and slight missing-of-the-point is perfect character work. Economy score is near-perfect.

jokes.text: Fuck. We're in deep shit. Yes, we are in very, very deep shit.
jokes.setup: Samir's 'my cousin's a cokehead' has revealed the depths of their uselessness
jokes.punchline: The escalating agreement — 'deep shit' → 'very, very deep shit' — is funny in its redundancy and the way three grown men solemnly agree on their own incompetence
jokes.explanation: Functional beat that lands as a capper to the exchange. The slight escalation ('very, very') is a minor craft touch. Doesn't reach beyond competent.

jokes.text: Lumbergh casually instructs Milton to get a flashlight and crawl down to handle cockroaches, cutting him off mid-protest
jokes.setup: Milton has just said cockroach extermination 'really isn't my job'
jokes.punchline: Lumbergh steamrolls right over the objection with cheerful corporate-speak ('it would be really great if you could just sort of...'), adding physical indignity (crawling with a flashlight)
jokes.explanation: Classic Lumbergh behavior — the passive-aggressive phrasing ('it would be really great') masking total dismissal of Milton. Character-integrated but familiar ground by this point in the film.

jokes.text: [Door closes] OK...but that's the last straw.
jokes.setup: Lumbergh has been pulled away before finishing his cockroach instructions; Milton stands alone
jokes.punchline: Milton solemnly declares 'that's the last straw' — a line the audience knows he's said (or thought) many times before, gaining dark comedy weight because we know the building will burn
jokes.explanation: The rewatch value is what elevates this — on first viewing it's a good character beat; on rewatch it's a perfectly placed dramatic irony beat. The deadpan finality of 'that's the last straw' after the door cuts him off is excellent economy. The pause (door closes, beat, 'OK') is itself funny. Close to the 8-anchor.

jokes.text: Here we go, here we go. Uh, launder. 'To clean,' no. 'To wash—' 'To conceal the source of money as by channeling it through an intermediary.'
jokes.setup: The trio established they don't know what money laundering means
jokes.punchline: Michael is literally looking it up in a physical dictionary — the most unhelpfully literal possible research method for planning a crime
jokes.explanation: The visual of three software engineers huddled around a dictionary to plan financial crime is a great comedic image. The payoff line from Samir — 'That doesn't really help us, Michael' — makes it a full comedic unit. Well-structured.

jokes.text: That doesn't really help us, Michael.
jokes.setup: Michael has just read the dictionary definition of money laundering aloud as if it were actionable information
jokes.punchline: Samir's flat, polite dismissal of the definition as unhelpful punctuates the absurdity perfectly
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — six words that land exactly right. The polite understatement ('doesn't really help us') in the face of complete criminal ineptitude is very funny. Samir's straight-man role is well-deployed here.

jokes.text: I can't believe what a bunch of nerds we are. We're looking up money laundering in a dictionary.
jokes.setup: The trio has just looked up 'launder' in a dictionary as a step toward committing financial crime
jokes.punchline: Peter breaks the fourth wall of their self-delusion by naming exactly what they're doing and how pathetic it is
jokes.explanation: Self-aware humor that works because it's exactly right. Peter articulating the absurdity they're living in is a good observational beat. The specific image of the dictionary is what makes it land — it's not just 'we're bad at crime' but a precise, embarrassing detail.

jokes.text: Yeah, well, you guys can both eat my ass, OK?
jokes.setup: Peter has just mocked Michael (and by extension himself) for the dictionary plan
jokes.punchline: Michael's defensive, slightly petulant comeback — delivered with Michael Bolton's particular brand of wounded pride — is funnier for its disproportionate indignation
jokes.explanation: Michael Bolton's thin-skinned defensiveness is a solid character note. The 'OK?' at the end adds a funny flustered quality. Not exceptional but character-consistent.

jokes.text: I can't believe Joanna slept with Lumbergh. That's what I can't believe.
jokes.setup: They're in crisis over embezzlement and possible prison; Michael pivots completely to Peter's romantic grievance
jokes.punchline: The total non-sequitur pivot from prison panic to romantic jealousy is the joke — Michael can't resist bringing this up even in a crisis
jokes.explanation: Good tonal whiplash gag — crisis pivot to petty gossip. Sets up the excellent 'Ron Lumbergh' misdirect coming in a few beats.

jokes.text: Yeah, you didn't know that? Yeah, you didn't know that? — both Samir and Michael piling on simultaneously
jokes.setup: Peter reacts to the Joanna/Lumbergh revelation
jokes.punchline: Both Samir and Michael simultaneously ask the same question, suggesting everyone knew but Peter — adding insult to injury
jokes.explanation: The simultaneous pile-on is a good beat that deepens Peter's humiliation. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: You mean Ron Lumbergh, the Initrode guy? The young guy?
jokes.setup: Peter has been quietly horrified believing Joanna slept with his awful boss Bill Lumbergh
jokes.punchline: He's been suffering over the wrong Lumbergh — there's a completely different, apparently acceptable Lumbergh — recontextualizing his entire jealousy
jokes.explanation: This is one of the better structural gags in the reel. The misdirection has been running since an earlier reel, and the payoff — an entirely different Lumbergh, a young guy at a competing company — is unexpected, cleanly structured, and recontextualizes everything. Peter's torment was based on a misunderstanding. The setup is long (earlier reels) which makes the payoff richer. Close to the 8-anchor quality.

jokes.text: Her fucking — her children would have hooves.
jokes.setup: The clarification that it was Ron, not Bill Lumbergh — implying what it would mean if it HAD been Bill
jokes.punchline: Michael's visceral, almost mythological horror at the thought of Joanna being with Bill Lumbergh — that their children would be literally demonic/animal — is a hyperbolic insult that lands hard
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the reel. The image of Lumbergh's children having hooves is startlingly original — it's not just an insult, it's a supernatural/demonic implication delivered with absolute commitment. The word 'hooves' is doing enormous work. Michael's disgust at Lumbergh expressed through this bizarre biological horror is perfectly economical and quotable. Comfortably above the 8-anchor threshold.

jokes.text: Ron's not related to Bill, is he?
jokes.setup: Michael has just said Joanna's children with Bill would have hooves; the group is processing the two-Lumbergh situation
jokes.punchline: Samir's cautious, slightly paranoid question — asking if the acceptable Lumbergh might be tainted by association with the monster — is a perfect deadpan beat
jokes.explanation: A compact, well-timed follow-up that extends the hooves joke's logic. The implied fear that any Lumbergh bloodline is contaminated is funny and consistent with the film's demonization of Bill Lumbergh.

jokes.text: Good evening, sir. My name is Steve. I come from a rough area. I used to be addicted to crack but now I'm off and trying to stay clean. That is why I'm selling magazine subscriptions.
jokes.setup: The trio anxiously opens the door expecting danger; instead it's a magazine salesman with a rehearsed poverty narrative
jokes.punchline: The formulaic, obviously-rehearsed sad-story pitch — delivered with door-to-door professionalism — is the joke, setting up a bigger reversal
jokes.explanation: Solid setup for the larger Steve joke. The overly polished poverty narrative is funny on its own, and the comedic relief of a magazine salesman after the tension of their crisis is well-timed.

jokes.text: I lied. All that stuff I said about being a crackhead just helps me sell magazines. I'm actually an unemployed software engineer.
jokes.setup: Steve has just been asked about knowing drug dealers; Michael had enthusiastically engaged with the crackhead story and was about to ask for contacts
jokes.punchline: The double reversal: Steve wasn't a crackhead (fake sales pitch), but IS a software engineer — the one identity that connects him to the trio and makes his con even stranger
jokes.explanation: This is a genuinely clever structural joke with two reversals. First: the crackhead story is fake (subverts expectations of authenticity). Second: he's actually a software engineer (connects him to the protagonists in the most absurd way possible). The specificity of 'software engineer' rather than any other job is the perfect comedic choice. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Things, they must be very rough for you. — Samir to the former software engineer turned magazine salesman
jokes.setup: Steve reveals he's an unemployed software engineer selling door-to-door
jokes.punchline: Samir's earnest, slightly condescending sympathy — directed at someone who is arguably doing better than them (they're facing federal prison) — is rich with dramatic irony
jokes.explanation: Samir's misplaced condescension — from men who are about to go to federal prison — is a good ironic beat. His formal diction ('they must be very rough for you') adds to the humor.

jokes.text: Actually, man, I make more money selling magazine subscriptions than I ever did at Initrode.
jokes.setup: Samir has just offered sympathy to Steve for being an unemployed software engineer
jokes.punchline: Steve casually reveals he earns more door-to-door than he did at the soul-crushing tech job, completely inverting Samir's pity
jokes.explanation: A satisfying beat that deepens the film's satirical point about the worthlessness of corporate tech jobs. The specificity of 'Initrode' (the rival company) ties it to the world. Well-structured reversal.

jokes.text: Actually, um, that all depends.
jokes.setup: Peter nervously asks Steve not to tell anyone about the money laundering conversation since they know the same people
jokes.punchline: Steve's casual, unhurried pivot to leverage — 'that all depends' — reveals he's going to blackmail them for magazine subscriptions
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — three words that completely reframe Steve as an opportunist. The beat before the reveal of what it 'depends' on is well-timed.

jokes.text: What am I gonna do with forty subscriptions to 'Vibe'?
jokes.setup: Steve has leveraged their secret for magazine subscriptions
jokes.punchline: The specific detail of 40 subscriptions to 'Vibe' magazine — a hip-hop/R&B publication — purchased by Michael Bolton (who famously shares a name with a soft-rock singer) is the comedic collision of specificity and absurdity
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Vibe' is brilliantly chosen — it's the magazine least likely to be wanted by these suburban white software engineers, and especially by Michael Bolton. The number '40' adds to the absurdity. This is comedy through precise, unexpected detail. Comfortably above the 8-anchor: it's compact, surprising, and highly quotable.

jokes.text: We never should have done this. What were we thinking? You know what I can't figure out? How is it that all these stupid Neanderthal Mafia guys can be so good at crime and smart guys like us can suck so badly at it?
jokes.setup: The trio has just been blackmailed by a magazine salesman for accidentally discussing money laundering
jokes.punchline: Peter's rhetorical question — the dumb criminals are better at crime than the smart engineers — is an honest, funny self-assessment that inverts the expected meritocracy
jokes.explanation: Good observational comedy that articulates the film's central comic premise. 'Neanderthal Mafia guys' is a vivid phrase. A bit overlong but the core insight is sharp.

jokes.text: No. We're going to federal 'pound me in the ass' prison.
jokes.setup: Peter distinguishes between 'white-collar resort prison' and what actually awaits them
jokes.punchline: The specific, lurid coinage 'pound me in the ass prison' — delivered with matter-of-fact precision — is the punchline, naming their fear in the most explicit and absurd possible terms
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable lines in the film. The setup ('not white-collar resort prison') is essential — it creates the contrast that makes 'pound me in the ass prison' land as the punchline. The clinical deadpan delivery of an extremely crude phrase is the comedic technique. The specificity and coinage elevate it well above the 8-anchor. It became a cultural touchstone of the film.

jokes.text: Why the hell did I do this? I've never done anything wrong in my whole life.
jokes.setup: Peter and Michael are arguing over how they got into this mess
jokes.punchline: Samir's indignant self-righteousness in the middle of their criminal conspiracy — 'I've never done anything wrong in my whole life' — is the joke, as he is literally currently a co-conspirator
jokes.explanation: Samir's good-immigrant self-image in direct contradiction with his current situation is a solid character beat. The irony is clear and plays well.

jokes.text: You are a very... bad person, Peter.
jokes.setup: The group is breaking up for the night; everyone is furious at Peter for getting them into this
jokes.punchline: Samir's formal, almost judicial condemnation — 'You are a very... bad person' — with that deliberate pause, is a classic understatement as finale
jokes.explanation: The formal diction and deliberate pause make this exceptionally funny as a scene ender. 'Very... bad person' is simultaneously inadequate and perfectly pointed. The ellipsis/pause is doing real comedic work. High quotability.

jokes.text: Lawrence, you awake? Yeah. You wanna come over? No, thanks, man. I don't want you fucking up my life, too.
jokes.setup: Peter, isolated and in trouble, reaches out to his neighbor Lawrence for company
jokes.punchline: Lawrence's blunt, unapologetic refusal — 'I don't want you fucking up my life, too' — is a perfect Lawrence line, honest to the point of brutality
jokes.explanation: Lawrence's brutal honesty is his defining trait and this is a perfect expression of it. The timing — through the wall, in darkness, no hesitation — is ideal. 'I don't want you fucking up my life, too' is a great line.

jokes.text: ...to a term of no less than four years in a federal 'pound me in the ass' prison.
jokes.setup: Peter's nightmare uses the exact phrase he coined earlier to describe their fate
jokes.punchline: The official legal verdict uses Peter's own crude coinage — 'pound me in the ass prison' — now delivered by a formal judge in full judicial authority
jokes.explanation: The callback is well-structured — Peter's fear becomes his nightmare reality with his own words echoed back through official channels. The juxtaposition of judicial formality with the crude phrase is funnier than the original.

jokes.text: Peter Gibbons... you've led a trite and meaningless life... and you're a very bad person.
jokes.setup: In the dream, the judge has sentenced Michael and Samir; now turns to Peter
jokes.punchline: Instead of a prison sentence, Peter gets an existential verdict — 'trite and meaningless life' — which is somehow more devastating than prison, plus the callback to Samir's earlier 'very bad person'
jokes.explanation: This is one of the standout jokes in the reel. The subversion of the dream sentencing — giving Peter a philosophical verdict instead of a prison term — is exactly the kind of dark, specific comedy Mike Judge excels at. The phrase 'trite and meaningless life' is an unusually precise and stinging formulation. The callback to Samir's 'very bad person' elevates it further. Well above the 8-anchor.

jokes.text: I got fired. What happened? I flipped off my boss. Some customers — actually, a line cook — but he just happened to be standing there.
jokes.setup: Peter asks why Joanna isn't at Chotchkie's anymore
jokes.punchline: The story of flipping off her boss deflates when she clarifies it was actually a line cook who happened to be standing there — her rebellion was accidental and misdirected
jokes.explanation: The self-correction mid-story ('some customers... actually a line cook') is a good comedic structure — the story diminishes in real time. Character-appropriate: Joanna's small act of rebellion was only semi-intentional. Well-constructed.

jokes.text: It wasn't even the right Lumbergh.
jokes.setup: Peter is apologizing to Joanna for getting jealous about her and Lumbergh
jokes.punchline: His apology includes the sheepish admission that he was jealous over the wrong Lumbergh — a callback to the Ron/Bill clarification — delivered as the most embarrassing possible coda to his jealousy
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — six words that do enormous work. Peter's humiliation is deepened by this admission, and it's the most compact possible way to close the Lumbergh misdirection. The deadpan delivery of this embarrassing fact in the middle of a heartfelt apology is funny.

jokes.text: BRIAN: Whoa! Hey, what's going on here? Get a room, you two! Ha ha!
jokes.setup: Peter and Joanna have just reconciled with a kiss in a parking lot
jokes.punchline: Brian the Flair Guy interrupts their tender moment with performative bro enthusiasm, completely misreading the room
jokes.explanation: Generic 'get a room' interruption — the joke is primarily Brian's character (insufferable, oblivious enthusiasm) rather than any craft in the line itself. Functions as a callback appearance for the character. The 'Ha ha!' adds nothing.

jokes.text: I hate that guy.
jokes.setup: Brian has just bellowed 'Get a room, you two!' during their reconciliation
jokes.punchline: Peter's flat, immediate, sincere statement — no escalation, no elaboration — is the perfect one-beat capper
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum economy. The simplicity and sincerity of 'I hate that guy' in a romantic moment is funny precisely because it's so unromantic and direct. The audience agrees completely, which creates the shared laugh. Economy score is perfect.

jokes.text: Milton's escalating list of grievances to the secretary: moved desk, no paycheck, stapler taken, garbage on desk, storage room B
jokes.setup: Milton approaches the receptionist area to complain about Lumbergh
jokes.punchline: The entire litany of wrongs — delivered in Milton's particular rambling, can't-stop-himself way — is the joke: each indignity is mundane but the accumulation is both comedic and reveals a genuinely mistreated person
jokes.explanation: Pure character comedy — Milton's voice and cadence are the joke as much as the content. The list form is structurally sound and the specificity of 'storage room B' and 'garbage on it' are good detail. Economy suffers slightly from the rambling nature, but that's intentional and character-appropriate.

jokes.text: I have to take my stapler back because I told him it's my stapler.
jokes.setup: Milton has been told to go back to his desk; he mutters to himself as he leaves
jokes.punchline: The circular logic of 'I have to take it back because I told him it's mine' — as if saying it makes it legally binding — is a perfect expression of Milton's inner world
jokes.explanation: Character integration is near-perfect — the circular self-justifying logic is quintessentially Milton. The delivery in mumble registers perfectly. The stapler is probably the most iconic object in the film and every reference to it lands.

jokes.text: Hey, Peter. Watch out for your cornhole, bud.
jokes.setup: Peter is saying goodbye to Lawrence before going to confess; it's a tender, farewell-ish exchange
jokes.punchline: Lawrence's send-off — practical, blunt, and crude advice about prison sexual assault — is the perfect Lawrence line: sincere, unembarrassed, and kind in its own crude way
jokes.explanation: This is one of the best lines in the reel. Lawrence's character is defined by this line — crude, sincere, completely unself-conscious, and genuinely caring in his own way. 'Cornhole, bud' is a spectacular word choice. The juxtaposition with Peter's serious march toward self-sacrifice makes the crudeness land harder. The callback to the prison fear thread is structural gold. Comfortably above the 8-anchor.

jokes.text: Holy shit. — Peter seeing the Initech building on fire
jokes.setup: Peter is walking to Initech to confess and return the money; he's been building toward a heroic self-sacrifice
jokes.punchline: The building is already on fire — the visual reveal makes Peter's entire plan moot and delivers the payoff of Milton's long-running threat
jokes.explanation: This is the best single comedic moment in the reel. The structural payoff is massive: every Milton threat, every 'last straw,' every mumbled resentment across the entire film pays off in one image. Peter's reaction ('Holy shit') is the perfect two-word response. The fire solves all their problems without any effort on their part, which is both a great joke and a perfect satirical statement about corporate karma. This approaches the 9.5-anchor territory for structural payoff.

jokes.text: You don't want that, Peter, man. That's toasted, man. — Lawrence dismissing something recovered from the fire; Peter: I think I know someone who might want this.
jokes.setup: In the rubble of the burned building, Peter finds something
jokes.punchline: Peter recognizes that whatever charred item remains from the fire has a home — almost certainly the charred remains of something Initech-related that someone (Milton?) would treasure
jokes.explanation: A decent mystery-box beat. The humor is in the implication — we don't know what it is yet, but Peter's calm identification of a recipient is funny. Reasonably well-structured teaser.

jokes.text: How's Penetrode? — Peter asking about Initrode; Michael: Initrode.
jokes.setup: Peter asks how Michael and Samir's new job is going
jokes.punchline: Peter deliberately (or accidentally) mispronounces/mishears 'Initrode' as 'Penetrode' — the obscene substitution earning a flat correction from Michael
jokes.explanation: A quick, well-timed gag. The childish substitution of 'Penetrode' and Michael's flat correction is funny in its economy. Slight but effective.

jokes.text: Yeah. I think the fire pretty much took care of everything.
jokes.setup: The group is wondering if they're going to be OK after all the embezzlement chaos
jokes.punchline: Michael's breezy 'the fire pretty much took care of everything' — treating arson and destruction of evidence as a convenient cleaner — is delivered with complete calm
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy and the casual understatement of 'pretty much took care of everything' about a building fire is a great dark comedy beat. The matter-of-factness is the comedic technique.

jokes.text: I wonder if the money burn up. It would be shame.
jokes.setup: Michael says the fire took care of everything; they're reflecting on their situation
