jokes.punchline: Samir's broken-English lament — 'it would be shame' — about the embezzled money they were trying to return being destroyed is a perfect character note: still calculating the financial loss even now
jokes.explanation: The grammatically imperfect delivery ('it would be shame') combined with the dark absurdity of mourning money that was stolen and was going to be returned anyway is a good character beat. Samir's pragmatism as his defining trait is well-served here.

jokes.text: This isn't so bad, huh? Making bucks, getting exercise, working outside. Fuckin' A.
jokes.setup: Peter is now working a physical outdoor job (demolition/construction) alongside Lawrence
jokes.punchline: The cheerful corporate-speak inventory of job benefits ('making bucks, getting exercise, working outside') applied to manual labor — followed by Lawrence's 'Fuckin' A' — is a funny contrast to Peter's white-collar suffering
jokes.explanation: Good thematic beat that completes Peter's arc while being genuinely funny. Lawrence's 'Fuckin' A' as the definitive endorsement is perfect character work. The contrast with the film's opening scenes of corporate misery is satisfying.

jokes.text: Milton at a beach resort complaining about drink orders: wrong mai tai, salt on the margarita — 'I won't be leaving a tip 'cause I could... I could shut this whole resort down.'
jokes.setup: Milton has apparently been rewarded (or escaped) and is now at a beach resort
jokes.punchline: Milton is doing to the resort waiter exactly what Lumbergh did to him — issuing passive-aggressive, euphemistic escalating threats — but framed as victimhood ('I asked for a mai tai')
jokes.explanation: A structural triumph: Milton has become the very thing that oppressed him, applying the same petty escalation of threats ('I could write a letter to your board of tourism... I could have this place condemned') to a resort waiter over drink garnishes. The parallel with Lumbergh is the meta-joke. High character integration, strong rewatch value.

jokes.text: I could put, I could put strychnine in the guacamole.
jokes.setup: Milton's threat escalation at the resort has gone through letter-writing and place-condemnation
jokes.punchline: The sudden jump to actual poisoning — 'strychnine in the guacamole' — is a massive, jarring escalation from petty consumer complaint to attempted murder, delivered in the same mild tone
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the reel and one of the best in the film. The comedic architecture is flawless: escalate from mild consumer complaint → letter writing → condemnation → murder threat, all in the same unassuming voice. The word 'strychnine' is the perfect word — specific, clinical, and completely at odds with 'guacamole.' Milton has not changed one bit despite his apparent freedom: he still escalates to mass murder over minor inconveniences. This approaches the 9.5-anchor territory for execution. The comedic logic is airtight.

jokes.text: There was salt on the glass, big grains of salt.
jokes.setup: Milton has just threatened to put strychnine in the guacamole
jokes.punchline: He immediately deflates from attempted-murder threat to returning to the original complaint about salt — the strychnine was apparently a heat-of-the-moment thing and the real grievance is the garnish
jokes.explanation: The perfect button to the strychnine joke. The comedic technique of escalating to murder then immediately retreating to the original petty complaint ('big grains of salt') is masterful structural comedy. The specificity of 'big grains of salt' — the most insignificant possible grievance — maximizes the contrast with the death threat. This is the actual punchline of the strychnine setup. Near the 9.5-anchor level for structure and economy.

jokes.text: DREW: Give a ride on the old bone roller coaster. Aaaah! — Drew in a car with a woman, apparently in an intimate context
jokes.setup: Drew appears briefly in the closing montage
jokes.punchline: Drew's crude self-narration ('bone roller coaster') of his own sexual activity, delivered with his characteristic enthusiasm, is a funny character-consistent beat
jokes.explanation: Crude character comedy that works primarily on Drew's personality. 'Bone roller coaster' is a decent phrase but the joke is more broad than craft-driven. Functional.

jokes.text: JOANNA: I'm working at Hooters now, you know, and it's very cool.
jokes.setup: The end-credits montage shows where characters have landed; Joanna has left the flair-obsessed Chotchkie's
jokes.punchline: She's replaced one objectifying restaurant chain with Hooters — the more explicit version — and describes it as 'very cool,' either missing or not caring about the irony
jokes.explanation: A compact, well-structured ironic beat. The logic of 'left one exploitative restaurant for a more explicitly exploitative one' is a sharp satirical observation delivered with complete sincerity. 'And it's very cool' is the killer phrase.

jokes.text: JOANNA: I'm working at Hooters now, you know... and it's very cool.
jokes.setup: The end credits montage shows where everyone ended up
jokes.punchline: Joanna, who quit Chotchkie's over its demeaning flair policy, is now working at Hooters — a restaurant whose entire concept is objectification — and finds it 'very cool'
jokes.explanation: The irony is sharp: Joanna left Chotchkie's because she objected to the performative expectations of the job, and her solution is Hooters, which has even more explicit performance expectations of a different kind. The fact that she finds it 'very cool' and means it is a funny character comment — she didn't object to the job itself, just to the specific form of corporate control. It's a small but well-observed satirical joke about how people rationalize their choices.

jokes.text: While the most hated get placed in some small cubicle spaces / Or get thrown down in the basement / Get your stapler confiscated, you constantly waitin' / For a paycheck, twelve months pass by and you still ain't get paid yet
